koike@phys.keio.ac.jp\n46\t}\n47\t%-------------------------------------------------------\n48\t%Contribution to workshop on\n49\t%ANALOG MODELS OF GENERAL RELATIVITY,\n50\t%Rio de Janeiro, 16-20 Oct., 2000\n51\t%-------------------------------------------------------\n52\t\\vskip 1.0 cm\n53\t\\noindent {\\bf Abstract:} \n54\t{\\it Condensed matter black hole analogues may provide guidance in\n55\tgrappling with difficult questions about the role of short distance\n56\tphysics in the Hawking effect.  These questions bear on the very\n57\texistence of Hawking radiation, the correlations it may or may not\n58\tcarry, the nature of black hole entropy, and the possible loss of\n59\tinformation when a black hole evaporates.  We describe a model of\n60\tblack hole formation and evaporation and the loss of information to a\n61\tdisconnected universe in a thin film of \\He3-A, and we explain why the\n62\texistence of Hawking radiation has not yet been demonstrated in this\n63\tmodel.}\n64\t\n65\t%------------------------------------------------------\n66\t\\vskip 1.5 cm\n67\t%------------------------------------------------------\n68\t\\noindent[Chapter for book, {\\it Artificial Black Holes}, \n69\teds. M. Novello, M. Visser, and G. Volovik (World Scientific,\n70\t2002), based on a talk by TJ at the Workshop on Analog Models \n71\tof General Relativity, held at CBPF in Rio de Janeiro, October\n72\t16-20, 2000.]\n73\t%------------------------------------------------------\n74\t% Ted's definitions\n75\t%------------------------------------------------------\n76\t\\def\\3He{${}^3$He}\n77\t\\def\\ra{\\rangle}\n78\t\\def\\la{\\langle}\n79\t\\def\\ua{\\uparrow}\n80\t\\def\\da{\\downarrow}\n81\t\\def\\rar{\\rightarrow}\n82\t\\def\\beq{\\begin{equation}}\n83\t\\def\\eeq{\\end{equation}}\n84\t\\def\\bea{\\begin{eqnarray}}\n85\t\\def\\eea{\\end{eqnarray}}\n86\t%------------------------------------------------------\n87\t\\def\\O{\\Omega}\n88\t%\\def\\mi{\\math{i}}\n89\t\\def\\mi{i}\n90\t\\def\\scri{{\\cal I}}\n91\t\\def\\eg{{\\emph{e.g.}}}\n92\t\\def\\d{{\\mathrm{d}}}\n93\t%------------------------------------------------------\n94\t\\section{Introduction and motivation}\n95\t%------------------------------------------------------\n96\tFrom the condensed matter point of view, black hole analogues are a\n97\tcuriosity. They certainly generate new questions, and they may lead to\n98\tnew insights into the interplay between bulk and microscopic physics.\n99\tFrom the quantum gravity point of view, there is much more at\n100\tstake. We are looking to condensed matter systems for the guidance\n101\tthey may provide in grappling with difficult questions about the role\n102\tof short distance physics in the Hawking effect. These questions bear\n103\ton the very existence of Hawking radiation, the correlations it may or\n104\tmay not carry, the nature of black hole entropy\\index{entropy}, and\n105\tthe possible loss of information when a black hole evaporates.\n106\t\n107\tAlthough the Hawking\\index{Hawking effect} effect is a low-energy\n108\tphenomenon for black holes much larger than the Planck mass, it cannot\n109\tbe deduced strictly within a low energy effective theory.  The\n110\tgravitational redshift from the event horizon is infinite, so the\n111\toutgoing modes that carry the Hawking radiation emerge from the\n112\tPlanck\\index{Planck regime} regime.  To derive the Hawking effect one\n113\tneeds only the assumption that near the horizon these modes emerge in\n114\ttheir local ground state at scales much longer than the Planck length\n115\tbut still much shorter than the black hole\n116\tradius~\\cite{TJcutoff}. This assumption is {\\it plausible}, since the\n117\tbackground is slowly varying in time and space compared to these\n118\tscales.  However, it is not {\\it derived}.\n119\t\n120\tA condensed matter analogy has already provided some support for this\n121\tpicture.  Unruh~\\cite{Ted-Unruh81} introduced a sonic\\index{acoustic\n122\tblack hole} analogue, in which the black hole is modeled by a fluid flow\n123\twith a supersonic ``horizon'', and the quantum field is replaced by\n124\tthe quantized perturbations of the flow.  In a continuum treatment,\n125\tUnruh argued that the horizon would radiate thermal\\index{thermal\n126\tphonons} phonons at the Hawking\\index{Hawking temperature} temperature\n127\t$\\hbar\\kappa/2\\pi$, where $\\kappa$, which would be the surface gravity\n128\tfor a black hole, is here the gradient of the velocity field evaluated\n129\tat the sonic horizon.  The short-distance (atomic) physics of this\n130\tanalogue is fully understood in principle, hence it should be possible\n131\tto understand the origin and state of the Hawking\\index{Hawking modes}\n132\tmodes. As a first step inspired by this model, a number of studies\n133\thave been carried out where the linearity of the quantum field\n134\tequation is preserved but the short distance behavior is modified\n135\teither by introducing nonlinear dispersion\\index{dispersion} or a\n136\tlattice\\index{lattice} cutoff\\index{cutoff}, designed to mimic some\n137\taspects of the real atomic fluid.  The consequences have been\n138\tdiscussed in detail elsewhere (see~\\eg~\\cite{river} for a review).\n139\tThe main point is that, despite the exotic origin of the outgoing\n140\tmodes via ``mode\\index{mode conversion} conversion'' near the horizon,\n141\tthe short-distance physics does indeed deliver these modes in their\n142\tlocal ground state near the horizon if they originate far from the\n143\thorizon in their ground state.  These models thus lend some (linear\n144\tbut nontrivial) support to the contention that Planck scale effects\n145\tdeliver the local vacuum at a black hole horizon.\n146\t\n147\tA controversial consequence of this simple picture, however, is that\n148\tthe Hawking\\index{Hawking effect} effect produces a loss of\n149\tinformation\\index{information loss} from the world outside the\n150\thorizon.  The reason is that the local vacuum condition at the horizon\n151\tentails correlations between the field fluctuations inside and outside\n152\tthe horizon.  The radiated Hawking\\index{Hawking quanta} quanta are\n153\tthus correlated to ``partners'' that fall into the black\n154\thole.\\footnote{In addition to the information of correlations between\n155\tHawking quanta and their partners, any information that simply falls\n156\tinto the black hole from the outside appears to be lost.}  The origin\n157\tof these correlations is precisely the same as in the vacuum of flat\n158\tspacetime, so it is difficult to see any reason to doubt this\n159\taccount. It is often doubted, however, since it implies that the\n160\tprocess of formation and complete evaporation of a black hole entails\n161\tnon-unitary evolution in the Hilbert\\index{Hilbert space} space\n162\trestricted to the outside world, which is considered by many (not\n163\tincluding the authors) to be a violation of quantum mechanics.  It\n164\twould be useful to have a down-to-earth condensed matter analogue in\n165\twhich the information loss question arises but the fundamental physics\n166\tis understood.\n167\t\n168\t\n169\tRelated to the issue of information loss is the nature of black hole\n170\tentropy\\index{entropy}.  A spherical black hole of mass $M$ emitting\n171\tan energy $\\d E=\\d M c^2$ in thermal radiation at the\n172\tHawking\\index{Hawking temperature} temperature $T_H=\\hbar c^3/8\\pi GM$\n173\tloses an entropy $\\d S = \\d E/T_H = \\d(A/4l_P^2)$, where $A=4\\pi\n174\tR_s^2$ is the area of the event horizon of radius $R_s=2GM/c^2$, and\n175\t$l_P=(\\hbar G/c^3)^{1/2}\\simeq10^{-33} {\\,\\rm cm}$ is the Planck\n176\tlength.  A black hole thus has one unit of entropy for every four\n177\tunits of Planck area.  To understand the nature of the microscopic\n178\tdegrees of freedom counted by this entropy remains one of the\n179\toutstanding problems of quantum black hole physics.  To solve this\n180\tproblem will presumably require understanding the nature of the\n181\tshort-distance cutoff\\index{cutoff}.  Without a cutoff the entropy\n182\twould seem to be infinite due to the quantum\n183\tentanglement\\index{entanglement} between field degrees of freedom on\n184\teither side of the event horizon discussed in the previous paragraph.\n185\tIf a condensed matter horizon analogue produces Hawking\\index{Hawking\n186\teffect} radiation, then it would seem to also carry an\n187\tentanglement\\index{entanglement} entropy\\index{entropy}, so it may\n188\tprovide some guidance on the nature of black hole entropy.  (There are\n189\timportant differences however, since in the condensed matter setting\n190\tthere is no relation between the energy of the system and the area of\n191\tthe horizon, the Einstein\\index{Einstein equation} equation of course\n192\tdoes not pertain to the evolution of the horizon area, and the area\n193\tneed not even change during the evolution of the system.)\n194\t\n195\tThe basic question of the existence of the Hawking\\index{Hawking\n196\teffect} effect, as well as the issues of information\\index{information\n197\tloss} loss and black hole entropy should be approachable in condensed\n198\tmatter analogues.  The system we focus on here is particularly\n199\tinteresting in that it provides a model of the formation and\n200\tevaporation of a black hole, with a disconnected part of the\n201\t``universe'', analogous to a so-called ``baby\\index{baby universe}\n202\tuniverse'', into which information can potentially be lost.\n203\t\n204\tIt should be stated at the outset that at this stage we have only a\n205\tmodel of the background spacetime geometry.  A detailed analysis of\n206\tissues pertaining to the Hawking\\index{Hawking effect} effect remains\n207\tto be carried out, and it is not yet clear that this system would\n208\tproduce analogue Hawking\\index{Hawking effect} radiation.  Another point\n209\tworth stressing is that, for the purposes of obtaining guidance in\n210\tquantum gravity issues, the experimental {\\emph{feasibility}} of\n211\tactually setting up and observing a condensed matter analogue is not\n212\tessential.  Nevertheless, experimental observations are certainly one\n213\tof the goals of the whole program, both to confirm the basic\n214\tproperties of the Hawking\\index{Hawking effect} effect, and to gain\n215\tinsight into the short-distance physics at play.\n216\t\n217\tIn the next section we introduce \\He3-A and discuss how this medium\n218\tcan be used to construct various black hole analogues.  This is followed\n219\tby a section focusing on the effective\\index{effective geometry}\n220\tgeometry and Hawking\\index{Hawking effect} radiation in the moving\n221\tthin-film domain-wall\\index{domain wall} model.  The last section\n222\tdescribes the analogue of black hole formation and evaporation and the\n223\tloss of information\\index{information loss} to a disconnected universe\n224\tin the that model. We would like this article to be accessible to\n225\tresearchers in both condensed matter and gravitational physics, hence\n226\twe include more than the usual amount of introductory material.  We\n227\tuse units with $k_B=1$.\n228\t\n229\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n230\t\\section{Black hole analogues using \\3He}\n231\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n232\t\n233\tThe Hawking\\index{Hawking effect} effect is a quantum tunneling\n234\tprocess that produces a gentle instability of the ground state due to\n235\tthe presence of unoccupied negative energy states in the\n236\tergoregion\\index{ergoregion} behind the horizon.  The instability\n237\tcreates a flux of particles in a thermal state at the\n238\tHawking\\index{Hawking temperature} temperature.  If a condensed matter\n239\tsystem is to produce identifiable analogue Hawking\\index{Hawking effect}\n240\tradiation, therefore, the system should presumably be at least be as\n241\tcold as the Hawking temperature,\\footnote{This condition may be\n242\tavoided by observing instead a runaway quantum instability related to\n243\tthe Hawking\\index{Hawking effect} effect that is expected to occur for\n244\tbosonic fields when there is an inner horizon in addition to an outer\n245\thorizon~\\cite{CJsuper,Anglin}.} which is very low temperature for\n246\treasonable laboratory parameters.  Moreover, there should be no other\n247\tdissipation mechanisms that could swamp the Hawking\\index{Hawking\n248\teffect} effect.\n249\t\n250\tA natural place to start looking is therefore at\n251\tsuperfluid\\index{superfluid} systems at zero temperature.  The case of\n252\tsuperfluid \\He4\\index{Helium~4} was initially examined in\n253\t\\cite{ultrashort}, and further discussed in \\cite{TJorigin}.  It was\n254\tconcluded that a sonic horizon cannot be established in superflow,\n255\tbecause the flow is unstable to roton creation at the\n256\tLandau\\index{Landau velocity} velocity which is some four times\n257\tsmaller than the sound velocity.\n258\t\n259\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n260\t\\subsection{\\3He-A}\n261\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n262\t\n263\tPotentially more promising~\\cite{JVhorizons,KVdecay,JVfilm,Vtorus} is\n264\tthe (anisotropic) A-phase of superfluid\\index{superfluid}\n265\t${}^3$He,\\index{Helium~3-A} which has a rich spectrum of massless\n266\tquasiparticle\\index{quasiparticle} excitations.  In particular, there\n267\tare fermionic quasiparticles\\index{quasiparticle} --- the ``dressed''\n268\thelium atoms --- which have gapless\\index{energy gap} excitations near\n269\tthe gap nodes at $\\vec{p}=\\pm p_{F}\\;\\hat{\\bm{l}}$ on the anisotropic\n270\tFermi surface, and therefore can play the role of a massless\n271\trelativistic field\\index{massless relativistic field} in a black hole\n272\tanalogue.  The unit vector $\\hat{\\bm{l}}$ is the direction of orbital\n273\tangular momentum of the $p$-wave Cooper\\index{Cooper pair} pairs and\n274\t$p_F$ is the Fermi\\index{Fermi momentum} momentum.\n275\t\n276\tFor the benefit of readers not familiar with \\3He-A we inject here a\n277\tlightning sketch of the basics.  (For complete introductions see\n278\t\\cite{VollWolf,Vexotic,Leggett}.)  \\3He is a spin-1/2 fermion, and is\n279\tdescribed in a many-body fluid by a second quantized field operator\n280\t$\\psi^A(x)$, where $A$ is a two-component spinor index.  The fluid has\n281\ta phase transition at 2.7 mK to a superfluid\\index{superfluid} state\n282\tin which the order parameter $\\la \\psi^A({\\bf x})\\,\\psi^B({\\bf y})\\ra\n283\t= f^{AB}({\\bf x}-{\\bf y})$ is non-zero.  Below a pressure of about 33\n284\tbars and a temperature of order 1 mK the fluid is in the so-called\n285\tB-phase.  The A-phase is a very long-lived metastable phase that is\n286\tcoexistent with the B-phase and is stable in the region between 20 and\n287\t33 bars from 2.7 mK down to around 2 mK at the higher pressure.  In\n288\tthe A-phase the order parameter, which can be thought of as the wave\n289\tfunction of a Cooper\\index{Cooper pair} pair, is a spatial p-wave and\n290\ta spin triplet, and has the structure $|L=1, m_L=1\\ra \\otimes\n291\t|S=1,m_S=0\\ra$.  The coherence\\index{coherence length} length $\\xi$,\n292\twhich corresponds to the size of the Cooper\\index{Cooper pair} pair\n293\twavefunction, is of order 500 \\AA.  The Fourier\\index{Fourier\n294\ttransform} transform of $f^{AB}({\\bf x}-{\\bf y})$ evaluated near the\n295\tFermi\\index{Fermi momentum} momentum $|{\\bf p}|=p_F$ is proportional\n296\tto the energy gap\\index{energy gap}\n297\t%\n298\t\\beq \n299\t\\Delta({\\bf p})={\\Delta\\over p_F}\\; \n300\t\\left({\\bf e}_1+i{\\bf e}_2\\right)^i\\, p_i \\;\n301\t{(|\\ua\\da\\ra+|\\da\\ua\\ra)\\over\\sqrt{2}},\n302\t\\label{E:gap}\n303\t\\eeq\n304\t%\n305\twhere the three unit vectors ${\\bf l}$, ${\\bf e}_1$ and ${\\bf e}_2$\n306\tform a right-handed orthonormal triad.  The gap\\index{energy gap}\n307\tfunction (\\ref{E:gap}) has nodes at $\\vec{p}=\\pm\n308\tp_F\\;\\hat{\\bm{l}}$. Near these nodes the fermion\n309\tquasiparticles\\index{quasiparticle} can have arbitrarily low energies\n310\t(above the Fermi\\index{Fermi energy} energy), and they behave like\n311\tmassless relativistic particles. The velocity of these quasiparticles\n312\tparallel to $\\hat{\\bm{l}}$ in ${}^3$He-A is the Fermi\\index{Fermi\n313\tvelocity} velocity $v_F\\sim 55$ m/s, while their velocity\n314\tperpendicular to $\\hat{\\bm{l}}$ is only $c_\\perp =\\Delta/p_F\\sim 3$\n315\tcm/s, where $\\Delta\\sim T_c\\sim 1$ mK is the energy gap\\index{energy\n316\tgap}.\n317\t\n318\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n319\t\\subsection{Black hole candidates}\n320\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n321\t\\subsubsection{Superflow}\n322\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n323\tIt should be possible to set up an inhomogeneous superflow exceeding\n324\tthe slow speed $c_\\perp$ in a direction normal to $\\hat{\\bm{l}}$, thus\n325\tcreating a horizon for the fermion\n326\tquasiparticles\\index{quasiparticle}.  There is a catch, however,\n327\tsince the superflow is unstable when the speed relative to a container\n328\texceeds $c_\\perp$~\\cite{KVdecay}.  A possible way around this was\n329\tsuggested by Volovik~\\cite{Vtorus}, who considered a thin film of\n330\t\\He3-A flowing\\index{flowing fluid} on a substrate of superfluid\\index{superfluid} \\He4, \n331\twhich insulates the \\He3 from contact with the container.  In such a\n332\tfilm, the vector ${\\bf l}$ is constrained to be perpendicular to the\n333\tfilm.  A radial flow on a torus, such that the flow velocity near the\n334\tinner radius exceeds $c_\\perp$, would produce a horizon.\n335\tTheoretically this looks promising, however the Hawking\\index{Hawking\n336\ttemperature} temperature for a torus of size $R$ is $T=\n337\t(\\hbar/2\\pi)(\\d v/\\d r)\\sim \\hbar c_\\perp/R\\sim (\\lambda_F/R)$ mK,\n338\twhere $\\lambda_F$ is the Fermi wavelength, which is of the order of\n339\tAngstroms.  Thus, even for a micron sized torus, the\n340\tHawking\\index{Hawking temperature} temperature would be only $\\sim\n341\t10^{-7}$ K.\n342\t\n343\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n344\t\\subsubsection{Moving solitonic texture}\n345\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n346\tAn alternative is to keep the superfluid\\index{superfluid} at rest\n347\twith respect to the container, but arrange for a texture in the order\n348\tparameter to propagate in such a way as to create a horizon.  For\n349\texample, in~\\cite{JVhorizons} a moving ``splay\n350\tsoliton''\\index{soliton} is considered.  This is a planar\n351\ttexture\\index{texture} in which the $\\hat{\\bm{l}}$ vector rotates from\n352\t$+\\hat{x}$ to $-\\hat{x}$ along the $x$-direction perpendicular to the\n353\tsoliton\\index{soliton} plane.  A quasiparticle\\index{quasiparticle}\n354\tmoving in the $x$-direction thus goes at speed $v_F$ far from the\n355\tsoliton and at speed $c_\\perp$ in the core\\index{core} of the soliton.\n356\tIf the soliton is moving at a speed greater than $c_\\perp$, the\n357\tquasiparticles will not be able to keep up with it, so an effective\n358\thorizon will appear.  This example turns out to be rather interesting\n359\tand complicated in the effective relativistic description.  The null\n360\trays on the horizon have a transverse velocity, making it like that of\n361\ta rotating black hole rather than a static black hole.  In addition,\n362\tsince the $\\hat{\\bm{l}}$ vector couples to the\n363\tquasiparticles\\index{quasiparticle} like an electromagnetic vector\n364\tpotential, its time and space dependence generates a strong\n365\t``pseudo-electromagnetic'' field outside the ``black hole'' which\n366\twould produce quasiparticle\\index{quasiparticle} pairs by analogy\n367\twith Schwinger pair production~\\cite{Vexotic}. (This latter process\n368\tmay be the same as what produces the so-called ``orbital\n369\tviscosity''~\\cite{VollWolf} of a time-dependent\n370\ttexture\\index{texture}.)  The Hawking\\index{Hawking temperature}\n371\ttemperature also tends to be very low, and it seems likely that the\n372\tHawking\\index{Hawking effect} effect would be masked by the\n373\tpseudo-Schwinger pair production, though this has not been\n374\tdefinitively analyzed.\n375\t\n376\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n377\t\\subsubsection{Thin film with a moving domain wall}\n378\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n379\tIn \\cite{JVfilm} a simpler system was studied, that of a thin film of\n380\t\\He3-A, perhaps on a \\He4 substrate, with a domain\\index{domain wall}\n381\twall.  The vector $\\hat{\\bm{l}}$, which is perpendicular to the film,\n382\thas opposite sign on either side of the wall, and in the wall region\n383\tthe condensate\\index{condensate} is in a different\n384\tsuperfluid\\index{superfluid} phase.  At the core\\index{core} of the\n385\twall the group velocity of the quasiparticles\\index{quasiparticle}\n386\tgoes to zero, so if the wall itself is moving, a horizon will appear.\n387\tFor the rest of this article we focus on this example.  The effective\n388\tspacetime geometry of this system was first studied in~\\cite{JVfilm}.\n389\tHere we extend that analysis to the case of a wall that accelerates\n390\tand then comes to rest again.\n391\t\n392\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n393\t\\section[Effective spacetime from a moving domain wall]\n394\t{Effective spacetime and Hawking effect from a moving domain wall texture}\n395\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n396\t\\subsection{Texture and spectrum}\n397\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n398\t\n399\tThe order parameter for a domain\\index{domain wall} wall\n400\ttexture\\index{texture} in a thin film is described by a\n401\tgap\\index{energy gap} function of the same form as (\\ref{E:gap}), with\n402\tthe unit vector ${\\bf e}_1$ replaced by something like $\\tilde{\\bf\n403\te}_1=\\tanh(x/d)\\;{\\bf e}_1$, where $d\\sim\\xi$ is the width of the\n404\twall.  Here it is assumed that the film lies in the x-y plane with the\n405\twall along the y-axis.  (See figure~\\ref{F:film}) The thickness of the\n406\tfilm should be not much more than the coherence\\index{coherence\n407\tlength} length $\\xi$ in order for the domain\\index{domain wall} wall\n408\tto be stable.\n409\t\n410\t\\begin{figure}[htb]\n411\t\\bigskip\n412\t\\centerline{\n413\t\\psfig{figure=F-ted-film.eps,angle=-90,height=4cm}}\n414\t\\caption[Thin-film domain-wall texture]{\\sl Thin-film domain-wall texture.}\n415\t\\label{F:film}\n416\t\\end{figure}\n417\t\n418\tThe quasiparticle\\index{quasiparticle} spectrum in the A-phase takes\n419\tthe form\n420\t\\beq\n421\tE^2({\\bf p})=v_F^2\\;(p-p_F)^2+c_\\perp^2\\;({\\bf e}_1\\cdot{\\bf p})^2+\n422\tc_\\perp^2\\;({\\bf e}_2\\cdot{\\bf p})^2.\n423\t\\label{E:spectrum} \n424\t\\eeq \n425\tThere is no excitation perpendicular to the thin film, hence we have\n426\t$p_z=p_F$, so\n427\t%\n428\t\\beq \n429\tp=\\sqrt{p_F^2+p_x^2+p_y^2}=p_F+ \\frac{1}{2p_F}(p_x^2+p_y^2)+\\cdots.  \n430\t\\eeq \n431\t%\n432\tUsing this expansion in (\\ref{E:spectrum}) together with the\n433\treplacement ${\\bf e}_1\\rightarrow\\tilde{\\bf e}_1$ we obtain the low\n434\tenergy spectrum for motion in the $x$--$y$ plane in the\n435\tdomain\\index{domain wall} wall texture\\index{texture}:\n436\t%\n437\t\\beq\n438\tE^2= c(x)^2\\;p_x^2+c_\\perp^2\\;p_y^2 + \n439\t\\frac{c_\\perp^2}{\\hbar^2}\\;\\xi^2\\;(p_x^2+p_y^2)^2+\\cdots.\n440\t\\label{E:xyspectrum}\n441\t\\eeq \n442\t%\n443\tIn the quartic term we have replaced $v_F/2\\Delta$ by $\\xi/\\hbar$, to\n444\twhich it is roughly equal.  The speed $c(x)$, defined by\n445\t%\n446\t\\beq c(x)=c_\\perp \\tanh(x/d),\n447\t\\label{E:c(x)}\n448\t\\eeq\n449\t%\n450\tgoes to zero at the core\\index{core} of the domain\\index{domain wall} wall.\n451\t\n452\tIn the low energy limit the quartic term is negligible and the\n453\tspectrum becomes that of a massless relativistic particle in two\n454\tdimensions.  The nonrelativistic quartic corrections become important\n455\tat higher energy, when the wavelength is of order the\n456\tcoherence\\index{coherence length} length $\\xi$.  Note that this is of\n457\torder 500 \\AA, much longer than the interatomic spacing.\\footnote{In\n458\tthe analogy with quantum gravity, it would appear that the Planck\n459\tscale should be identified with $\\xi$ since this measures the\n460\t``elasticity'' of the background, and there is at present no analogue\n461\tof the underlying atomic scale in fundamental theory except perhaps\n462\tthe string scale, which is usually taken to be {\\it longer} than the\n463\tPlanck length, rather than shorter.} The corrections produce\n464\t``superluminal''\\index{superluminal} group velocities at high\n465\tmomentum.  If a quasiparticle\\index{quasiparticle} is {\\it localized}\n466\tnear the domain\\index{domain wall} wall then these nonrelativistic\n467\tcorrections are important, since the width of the wall is of order\n468\t$\\xi$.\n469\t\n470\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n471\t\\subsection{Spacetime of the stationary wall}\n472\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n473\t\\label{S:statwall}\n474\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n475\tThe relativistic limit of (\\ref{E:xyspectrum}) is that of a massless\n476\tparticle in a 2+1 dimensional spacetime with the line\n477\telement\\index{line element}\n478\t%\n479\t\\beq\n480\t\\d s^2=-\\d t^2 + c(x)^{-2}\\d x^2 + c_\\perp^{-2}\\d y^2.\n481\t\\eeq\n482\t%\n483\tThe metric has translation invariance in the y-direction, so we will\n484\tmake a ``dimensional reduction'' to the 1+1 dimensional spacetime\n485\t%\n486\t\\beq\n487\t\\d s^2 = -\\d t^2 + c(x)^{-2}\\d x^2.\n488\t\\label{E:rest}\n489\t\\eeq\n490\t%\n491\tClearly this spacetime is {\\it flat}, since one can introduce a new\n492\tspatial coordinate by $\\d x_*=\\d x/c(x)$ in terms of which the line\n493\telement takes the manifestly flat form $\\d s^2 = -\\d t^2 +\\d\n494\tx_*^2$. Note however that since $c(x)$ goes to zero linearly as\n495\t$x\\rightarrow0^+$, the coordinate $x_*$ goes to $-\\infty$\n496\tlogarithmically as the domain\\index{domain wall} wall is approached\n497\tfrom the side of positive $x$. Therefore the film really corresponds\n498\tto {\\it two complete copies} of flat spacetime, joined ``at infinity''\n499\tat the wall.\n500\t\n501\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n502\t\\subsection{Spacetime of the moving wall}\n503\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n504\t\\label{S:movewall}\n505\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n506\tNow suppose the domain\\index{domain wall} wall texture\\index{texture}\n507\tis moving to the right at speed $v<c_\\perp$ relative to the\n508\tsuperfluid\\index{superfluid} condensate\\index{condensate}.  Then right\n509\tmoving quasiparticles\\index{quasiparticle} sufficiently far from the\n510\twall will stay ahead of the wall, but those inside the point where\n511\t$c(x)=v$ will fail to stay ahead.  There will be a black hole horizon\n512\twhere $c(x)=v$ and a white hole\\index{white hole} horizon where\n513\t$c(x)=-v$ on the left hand side of the wall.  In between the two\n514\thorizons all low energy quasiparticles\\index{quasiparticle} are\n515\tpurely left-moving relative to the wall texture\\index{texture} (see\n516\tfigure~\\ref{F:vwall}).  The closer $v$ is to $c_\\perp$ the farther\n517\tapart the horizons lie.\n518\t%\n519\t\\begin{figure}[htb]\n520\t\\bigskip\n521\t\\centerline{\n522\t\\psfig{figure=F-ted-vwall.eps,angle=0,height=3cm}}\n523\t\\caption[Quasiparticles in a moving domain-wall texture]\n524\t{\\sl Quasiparticles in a moving domain-wall texture.}\n525\t\\label{F:vwall}\n526\t\\end{figure}\n527\t\n528\t\n529\tTo determine the spacetime metric for the moving wall, we introduce\n530\tcoordinates $x_s$ and $x_w$ at rest with respect to the\n531\tsuperfluid\\index{superfluid} and the wall, respectively.  These are\n532\trelated by the Galilean\\index{Galilean relativity} transformation\n533\t$x_s=x_w+vt$.  The dispersion\\index{dispersion relation} relation is\n534\tdetermined in the superfluid\\index{superfluid} frame, so the line\n535\telement\\index{line element} (\\ref{E:rest}) applies in the superfluid\n536\tframe, however the argument of the function $c(x)$ should be $x_w$\n537\tsince this function describes the texture\\index{texture} which is at\n538\trest in the wall frame.  For the moving wall we thus have\n539\t%\n540\t\\bea\n541\t\\d s^2\n542\t&=&-\\d t^2+c(x_w)^{-2}\\d x_s^2\\\\\n543\t&=&-\\d t^2+c(x_w)^{-2}(\\d x_w+v\\d t)^2\\\\\n544\t&=&-(1-v^2c(x_w)^{-2})\\d t^2 + \n545\t2vc(x_w)^{-2}\\,\\d t\\,\\d x_w +c(x_w)^{-2}\\d x_w^2.\n546\t\\label{E:movingwall}\n547\t\\eea\n548\t%\n549\tPerhaps surprisingly, this is no longer a flat spacetime.  It has\n550\tblack and white hole\\index{white hole} horizons at $c(x_h)=\\pm v$.\n551\tThe wall core\\index{core} at $x_w=0$ is now a {\\it spacelike} line\n552\t(since the coefficient of $\\d t^2$ is positive there), and it lies at\n553\t{\\it finite} proper time along geodesics.  The Ricci curvature scalar\n554\tis given by\n555\t%\n556\t\\beq\n557\tR=\\frac{-4v^2}{d^2}\\left(\\frac{c_\\perp^2}{c(x_x)^2}- \n558\t\\frac{c(x_x)^2}{c_\\perp^2}\\right).\n559\t\\eeq\n560\t%\n561\tThis diverges like $-(2v/x_w)^2$ as $x_w=0$ is approached, so there is\n562\ta curvature singularity at the core\\index{core}.  The spacetime\n563\ttherefore looks rather like that of an eternal Schwarzschild black\n564\thole.  The curvature at the horizon is given by\n565\t%\n566\t\\beq\n567\tR_{\\mathrm{horizon}} = -(2c_\\perp/d)^2\\;[1-(v/c_\\perp)^4].\n568\t\\eeq\n569\t%\n570\t\n571\tUnlike the maximally extended Schwarzschild black hole, however, the\n572\tspacetime of the moving wall is {\\it incomplete}, in that geodesics\n573\tcan run off the edge of the coordinate system $(t,x_w)$ in a finite\n574\tproper time or affine parameter.  The location of the incomplete\n575\tboundaries will be indicated below.  Of course physical\n576\tquasiparticles\\index{quasiparticle} cannot escape, because this\n577\treally is the entire physical spacetime.  What happens is that as a\n578\tquasiparticle heads in the direction of an incomplete boundary (either\n579\tforward or backward in time), it is blueshifted into the part of the\n580\tspectrum where the nonrelativistic corrections become important, at\n581\twhich point it propagates superluminally\\index{superluminal} and the\n582\tgeodesics of the effective metric no longer determine its trajectory.\n583\t\n584\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n585\t\\subsection{Hawking effect}\n586\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n587\t\\label{SS:hawking}\n588\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n589\tSince the effective spacetime is that of a black hole, it is natural\n590\tto suppose the horizon would radiate fermion\n591\tquasiparticles\\index{quasiparticle} at the Hawking\\index{Hawking\n592\ttemperature} temperature $T_H=(\\hbar/2\\pi)\\kappa$, where $\\kappa=\\d\n593\tc/\\d x(x_h)$ is the surface gravity of the horizon.  For the metric\n594\t(\\ref{E:movingwall}) with (\\ref{E:c(x)}) we have explicitly\n595\t%\n596\t\\beq\n597\tT_H(v)=T_H(0)\\;(1-v^2/c_\\perp^2),\\qquad\\qquad  \n598\tT_H(0)={\\hbar c_\\perp\\over2\\pi d}.\n599\t\\label{E:TH}\n600\t\\eeq\n601\t%\n602\tPutting in the numbers we have $T_H(0)\\sim 1 \\;\\mu$K. Equation\n603\t(\\ref{E:TH}) gives the Hawking\\index{Hawking temperature} temperature\n604\tin the wall reference frame (the ``Killing\\index{Killing temperature}\n605\ttemperature'' in the language of general relativity), which is related\n606\tto the temperature in the asymptotic frame of the\n607\tsuperfluid\\index{superfluid} by a Doppler\\index{Doppler effect} shift\n608\tfactor:\n609\t%\n610\t\\beq\n611\tT_{H, sf}=T_H(0)\\;(1+v/c_\\perp).\n612\t\\label{E:Tsf}\n613\t\\eeq\n614\t%\n615\tThe Hawking\\index{Hawking temperature} temperature in the frame of the\n616\tsuperfluid\\index{superfluid} is thus never less than $T_H(0)$.\n617\tAlthough this is three orders of magnitude below the\n618\tcritical\\index{critical temperature} temperature, and extremely low in\n619\tpractical terms, it is nevertheless close to where the\n620\tnon-relativistic corrections become important (assuming $d\\sim\\xi$).\n621\t\n622\tWhile the black hole analogy looks compelling, it should be emphasized\n623\tthat the Hawking\\index{Hawking effect} effect depends on behavior of\n624\tthe quantum field that may not be valid in this context.  As discussed\n625\tin the introduction, the required condition is that the high frequency\n626\toutgoing modes near the horizon be in their quantum ground state.  In\n627\tthis case these modes come from the singularity, since they propagate\n628\t``superluminally''\\index{superluminal}.  The propagation of these\n629\tmodes though the singularity may excite them.  This has not yet been\n630\tanalyzed.\\footnote{However the related problem of\n631\tquasiparticle\\index{quasiparticle} tunneling across the stationary\n632\tdomain\\index{domain wall} wall has been studied by Volovik in section\n633\t11.1 of \\cite{VolovikPR}.} If they are excited, this may suppress the\n634\tHawking\\index{Hawking effect} radiation by virtue of the\n635\tPauli\\index{Pauli principle} principle.  (Had the field been bosonic,\n636\tthe excitations would have produced extra, induced emission.)  Another\n637\tdifference from the black hole case is that once a\n638\tHawking\\index{Hawking pair} pair is produced, the negative energy\n639\tpartner rattles around trapped in the ergoregion\\index{ergoregion}\n640\tbetween the two horizons.  Once these available states fill up further\n641\tHawking\\index{Hawking effect} radiation would be suppressed.  (In the\n642\tcase of a black hole, by contrast, the negative energy partners fall\n643\tinto the singularity never to return.) For a discussion of aspects of\n644\tthe behavior of superfluids\\index{superfluid} in the presence of a\n645\tquasiparticle\\index{quasiparticle} horizon see\n646\treference~\\cite{VolovikPR}.\n647\t\n648\tFor the remainder of this article we assume that, in spite of\n649\tPauli-blocking effects, the moving domain\\index{domain wall} wall\n650\tproduces at least some Hawking\\index{Hawking effect} radiation, and we\n651\tgo on to study the analogue of the process of formation and\n652\tevaporation of a black hole. According to (\\ref{E:TH}) the\n653\tHawking\\index{Hawking temperature} temperature approaches a nonzero\n654\tconstant as $v\\rightarrow0$. Nevertheless it is clear that at $v=0$\n655\tthere can be no radiation since the wall is static and there is no\n656\thorizon, hence there is no ergoregion\\index{ergoregion} with negative\n657\tenergy states to be filled. The radiation rate must therefore go to\n658\tzero as $v$ goes to zero. If it goes as a power of $v$ then we have\n659\t$\\d E/\\d t = -b\\;v^n$. The kinetic energy of the moving\n660\tdomain\\index{domain wall} wall is proportional to $v^2$ if, as seems\n661\tplausible, the action is dominated by quadratic terms in the time and\n662\tspace derivatives. In this case $E=\\mu v^2/2$ for some constant\n663\t$\\mu$. Integrating the energy loss, we find that it takes a finite\n664\ttime for the wall to come to rest if $n<2$, but an infinite time if\n665\t$n\\ge2$.\n666\t\n667\tFinally, a comment about entropy\\index{entropy}.  It is tempting to\n668\ttry and define a thermodynamic entropy\\index{entropy} $S$ for the\n669\tmoving domain\\index{domain wall} wall, however it is by no means clear\n670\tthat this should be meaningful.  In analogy to the black hole entropy,\n671\tone might define $S$ via $\\d S = \\d E/T_{H, sf}$, where $E= \\mu v^2/2$\n672\tas above and $T_{H,sf}$ is the Hawking\\index{Hawking temperature}\n673\ttemperature in the superfluid\\index{superfluid} frame, (\\ref{E:Tsf}).\n674\tThis yields the formula $S=(2\\pi\\mu c_{\\perp}d/\\hbar)\\;\n675\t\\left(v/c_\\perp -\\ln(1+v/c_\\perp)\\right)$.  This analogy seems flawed\n676\thowever, as the domain\\index{domain wall} wall is not stationary in\n677\tthe superfluid\\index{superfluid} frame so does not represent an\n678\t``equilibrium'' system.  If we try to correct this by passing to the\n679\tframe of the moving wall, we run into the problem that, as the wall\n680\tslows down due to Hawking\\index{Hawking effect} radiation, this\n681\tcomoving frame {\\it changes}, unlike in the black hole case where the\n682\tasymptotic rest frame of the black hole is fixed even as the black\n683\thole evaporates (or absorbs radiation).\n684\t\n685\t\n686\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n687\t\\section[Hawking effect in the thin-film domain-wall model]\n688\t{Black hole formation and evaporation in the \n689\tthin-film domain-wall model}\n690\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n691\t\\subsection{Carter--Penrose causal diagrams}\n692\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n693\t\n694\tTo best exhibit the incompleteness of the black hole spacetime\n695\tdiscussed in the previous section, as well as features of the case\n696\twhere the hole forms and then evaporates, it is helpful to use\n697\tCarter--Penrose diagrams.  We therefore pause here to explain what\n698\tsuch a diagram is for the benefit of readers from the condensed matter\n699\tside.\n700\t\n701\tThe basic idea is to draw a picture representing the causal structure\n702\tof a spacetime by showing light rays at 45$^\\circ$, with regions at\n703\tinfinite time or space brought into a finite location by a spacetime\n704\tdependent conformal rescaling of the line element\\index{line element},\n705\t$\\d\\tilde{s}^2 =\\O^2 \\; \\d s^2$, where $\\O\\rar 0$ at infinity.  Since\n706\tthe causal structure is determined by the light cones, which are the\n707\tsolutions of $\\d s^2=0$, the causal structure of $\\d\\tilde{s}^2$ is\n708\tidentical to that of $\\d s^2$.  (See for example~\\cite{HawkEllis}.)\n709\t\n710\t\n711\tAs an example, consider 1+1 dimensional flat spacetime given by the\n712\tline element\\index{line element} $\\d s^2=-\\d t^2 +\\d x^2 = -\\d u \\, \\d\n713\tv$, where $u=t-x$ and $v=t+x$.  The conformal factor $\\O(u,v)=(\\cosh u\n714\t\\cosh v)^{-1}$ brings infinity into a finite location in the sense\n715\tthat the points at infinity for $\\d s^2$ lie at a finite proper distance\n716\tfor $\\d \\tilde{s}^2$.  A diagram of the tilde spacetime is then just a\n717\tdiamond, figure~\\ref{F:CP}\\,(a).  The boundaries of the spacetime are\n718\tat infinite time and/or space.  Timelike geodesics (straight lines in\n719\tthis case) emerge from past timelike infinity $\\mi^-$ and terminate at\n720\tfuture timelike infinity $\\mi^+$.  Spacelike geodesics go from left\n721\tspacelike infinity $\\mi^0_L$ to right spacelike infinity $\\mi^0_R$,\n722\tand null geodesics or light rays go from left or right past null\n723\tinfinity $\\scri^-$ (``scri-minus'') to right or left future null\n724\tinfinity $\\scri^+$ (``scri-plus'').\n725\t\n726\t\\begin{figure}[tbh]\n727\t\\centerline{\n728\t\\psfig{figure=F-ted-cartpen.eps,angle=0,height=10cm}}\n729\t\\caption[Carter--Penrose diagrams]{\\sl Carter--Penrose diagrams.}\n730\t\\label{F:CP}\n731\t\\end{figure}\n732\t\n733\tIn four-dimensional flat spacetime the spherical symmetry can be used\n734\tto reduce to a two dimensional diagram.  In spherical coordinates the\n735\tmetric is $\\d s^2=-\\d t^2 + \\d r^2 + r^2(\\d\\theta^2 + \\sin^2\\theta\\,\n736\t\\d\\phi^2)$.  If we now define $u =t-r$ and $v=t+r$, the geometry of\n737\tthe $t$-$r$ subspace for each set of polar angles is identical to the\n738\t1+1 dimensional case except that now only $v>u$ is physical.  The\n739\tspacetime is thus represented by figure~\\ref{F:CP}\\,(b), a diagram\n740\tthat is half of a diamond, with each point representing a 2-sphere\n741\texcept those on the vertical line on the left, which represents $r=0$.\n742\tThis is shown as a dotted line.\n743\t\n744\tThe spacetime of spherical matter that collapses to form a black hole\n745\tlooks like figure~\\ref{F:CP}\\,(c).  The shaded region represents the\n746\tcollapsing matter.  The dashed line represents the event horizon, and\n747\tthe thick-dashed line represents the curvature singularity inside the\n748\tblack hole.  Note that the singularity is {\\it spacelike}, and is the\n749\tfuture terminus of any causal curve that goes beyond the horizon.  It\n750\tis unknown how or even if spacetime develops in any form to the future\n751\tof the singularity, so a question mark is placed there.  One common\n752\thypothesis is that a ``baby\\index{baby universe} universe'' is born\n753\tthere, which is disconnected from the outside world.  A controversial\n754\tquestion is whether such a baby\\index{baby universe} universe can\n755\tharbor information\\index{information loss} unavailable to the outside\n756\tworld.\n757\t\n758\tThe diagram for a black hole that forms by collapse and then\n759\tevaporates away is shown in figure~\\ref{F:CP}\\,(d). After the black\n760\thole is gone, the origin of spherical coordinates appears shifted over\n761\tin the diagram.  No spacelike slice can enter the upper diamond\n762\t(region $F$) and still be a Cauchy\\index{Cauchy surface} surface,\n763\tsince causal curves that cross the horizon into the black hole will\n764\tnever reach such a surface. This is the basis of the claim that only\n765\tincomplete information is available to observers outside the horizon\n766\tafter the black hole is gone.\n767\t\n768\tOutside the matter the spacetime is the static Schwarzschild\n769\tline\\index{line element} element, which can be analytically extended\n770\tto a complete spacetime, the diagram of which is given in\n771\tfigure~\\ref{F:CP}\\,(e).  This so-called ``eternal'' black hole\n772\tspacetime is time-symmetric, with a white hole\\index{white hole}\n773\tsingularity in the past to match the black hole singularity in the\n774\tfuture.  It has two asymptotic spatial regions, connected through a\n775\t``throat''\\index{throat} at the center of the diagram.\n776\t\n777\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n778\t\\subsection{Diagrams of static and uniformly moving walls}\n779\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n780\t\\subsubsection{Static wall}\n781\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n782\tAs explained in section~\\ref{S:statwall} the spacetime of the static\n783\twall is just two complete copies of Minkowski spacetime.  The causal\n784\tdiagram is figure~\\ref{F:statwall}. In strictly relativistic terms\n785\tthere is no connection at all between the two spacetimes, however the\n786\tquasiparticles\\index{quasiparticle} can travel\n787\tsuperluminally\\index{superluminal} and thus pass from one side of the\n788\twall to the other at a finite value of the time coordinate $t$.  We\n789\tindicate this physical connection by depicting the spacetimes as\n790\tjoined at the wall at spatial infinity.\n791\t\n792\t\\begin{figure}[tbh]\n793\t\\centerline{\n794\t\\psfig{figure=F-ted-wallrest.eps,angle=0,height=3cm}}\n795\t\\caption[Static wall]{\\sl Static wall.}\n796\t\\label{F:statwall}\n797\t\\end{figure}\n798\t\n799\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n800\t\\subsubsection{Moving wall}\n801\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n802\tThe causal structure of the spacetime of the moving wall\n803\t(\\ref{E:movingwall}) is shown in figure~\\ref{F:movewall}\\,(a).  It\n804\tlooks like what one would obtain by cutting the diagram for the\n805\teternal black hole (figure~\\ref{F:CP}\\,(e)) along the white\n806\thole\\index{white hole} horizon, and sliding the lower half up so that\n807\tthe white hole\\index{white hole} singularity coincides with the black\n808\thole singularity.  The result of this cut is to leave the spacetime\n809\tincomplete along the cut, which corresponds to the pair of long-dashed\n810\tlines in figure~\\ref{F:movewall}\\,(a).  Geometrically it is not\n811\twell-defined to extend the spacetime across the singularity, but\n812\tphysically in the thin film there is continuity in passing through the\n813\tcore\\index{core} of the domain\\index{domain wall} wall.  The other\n814\tside of the wall thus plays the role of a baby\\index{baby universe}\n815\tuniverse.\n816\t\n817\tTo clarify the relation between the conformal diagram and the physical\n818\tspacetime we include in figure~\\ref{F:movewall}\\,(a) lines of constant\n819\t$t$, $x_s$, and $x_w$.  Note that the incomplete boundaries are at\n820\t$t\\rar \\pm\\infty$.  They are the terminus of a null ray that runs\n821\tparallel to the black hole horizon backward in time, or the white\n822\thole\\index{white hole} horizon forward in time.  Such null rays\n823\tasymptotically approach the horizon, blueshifting until\n824\tsuperluminal\\index{superluminal} terms in the\n825\tdispersion\\index{dispersion relation} relation become important, at\n826\twhich stage a quasiparticle\\index{quasiparticle} would cross the\n827\thorizon.  Note also that the Newtonian time slices cross the\n828\tsingularity progressively from left to right.\n829\t\n830\t\\begin{figure}[p]\n831\t\\centerline{\n832\t\\psfig{figure=F-ted-wallmove.eps,angle=-90,height=18cm}}\n833\t\\caption[Causal diagrams of moving domain-wall textures.]\n834\t{\\sl Causal diagrams of moving domain-wall textures.}\n835\t\\label{F:movewall}\n836\t\\end{figure}\n837\t\n838\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n839\t\\subsection{Black hole creation and evaporation}\n840\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n841\t\\subsubsection{Creation}\n842\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n843\tTo construct an analogue of a black hole that forms by collapse we\n844\timagine that the wall velocity $v$ is now a function of Newtonian time\n845\t$v(t)$ which is equal to zero before $t_1$ and thereafter smoothly\n846\tapproaches $v$.  (We do not attempt at this stage to devise a\n847\tmechanism for actually accelerating the wall in this manner.)  The\n848\tresulting spacetime should look like a portion of the static wall\n849\tfigure~\\ref{F:statwall} below $t_1$ and a portion of the moving wall\n850\tfigure~\\ref{F:movewall}\\,(a) above $t_1$.  This yields\n851\tfigure~\\ref{F:movewall}\\,(b).  Note that the past incomplete boundary\n852\tis now absent because the black hole forms at a finite time.\n853\t\n854\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n855\t\\subsubsection{Evaporation}\n856\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n857\tIn the case of a real black hole the energy for the\n858\tHawking\\index{Hawking effect} radiation comes from the mass of the\n859\thole.  As the hole radiates it loses mass until it evaporates away\n860\tcompletely, unless stabilized by conserved charges it cannot shed.  In\n861\tthe case of the domain\\index{domain wall} wall, the radiation occurs\n862\tonly when the wall is moving, and it is possible that the\n863\tback-reaction to the radiation causes the wall to slow down.  On the\n864\tother hand, as discussed in subsection~\\ref{SS:hawking}, Pauli\n865\tblocking may well terminate the Hawking\\index{Hawking effect} process\n866\tbefore the wall comes to rest.  There is presumably another\n867\tdissipation mechanism, such as pair-breaking due to the\n868\ttime-dependence of the moving texture\\index{texture}, that eventually\n869\twould stop the wall.  In any case, for the purposes of creating a\n870\tmodel of black hole evaporation, we can imagine simply that somehow or\n871\tanother the wall comes to rest at a time $t_2$.  The resulting\n872\tspacetime should then again look like a portion of the static wall\n873\tabove $t_2$, as shown in figure~\\ref{F:movewall}\\,(c).\n874\t\n875\tThe causal structure for the wall that accelerates and then stops is\n876\tsimilar but not entirely analogous to the spacetime of a black hole\n877\tthat evaporates.  There is no region analogous to region $F$ of\n878\tfigure~\\ref{F:CP}\\,(d), and in fact the spacetime is globally\n879\thyperbolic\\index{hyperbolic}.  The analogy is improved if we lean on\n880\tthe role of the Newtonian simultaneity to define what is accessible\n881\t``at a given time''.  Thus, subsequent to $t_2$, the spacetime\n882\tconsists again of two causally disconnected pieces analogous to $F$\n883\tand the black hole interior of figure~\\ref{F:CP}\\,(d).\n884\t\n885\tTo understand better what is going on it is helpful to use also a\n886\tnon-conformal diagram, in which the domain\\index{domain wall} wall\n887\tworldline is drawn vertically, figure~\\ref{F:window}.  The singularity\n888\tappears when the wall starts moving, and disappears when it comes to\n889\trest.  During the motion the singularity is a window to the other side\n890\tof the wall.  Figure~\\ref{F:window} shows the black and white\n891\thole\\index{white hole} horizons as dashed lines, as well as a\n892\tquasiparticle\\index{quasiparticle} worldline that crosses from right\n893\tto left, and a Hawking\\index{Hawking pair} pair that is created at the\n894\ttemporary horizon.\n895\t%\n896\t\\begin{figure}[htp]\n897\t\\centerline{\n898\t\\psfig{figure=F-ted-window.eps,angle=0,height=8cm}}\n899\t\\caption[Temporary one-way window]{\\sl Temporary one-way window.}\n900\t\\label{F:window}\n901\t\\end{figure}\n902\t%\n903\tNote that as it approaches the white hole\\index{white hole} horizon,\n904\tthe partner of the Hawking\\index{Hawking quantum} quantum is turned\n905\tback toward the singularity since it is rightmoving with respect to\n906\tthe superfluid\\index{superfluid} condensate\\index{condensate}. It\n907\t``rattles'' back and forth between the horizons until the wall stops\n908\tmoving.\n909\t\n910\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n911\t\\subsection{Information loss}\n912\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n913\t\n914\tIt seems clear from the previous discussion that\n915\tquasiparticle\\index{quasiparticle} information can fall across the\n916\thorizon and be lost to the outside world.  The information {\\it could}\n917\tcome back carried by superluminal\\index{superluminal} high energy\n918\tquasiparticles\\index{quasiparticle}, but it {\\it need not} and there\n919\tis no reason to suppose it does.  The question of information loss by\n920\tHawking\\index{Hawking effect} radiation is thornier.  The partners\n921\tremain in the ergoregion\\index{ergoregion} and fill the negative\n922\tenergy states.  It seems that roughly half their information would\n923\twind up on the right side of the singularity to be available after the\n924\tblack hole ``evaporates''.  Still, that leaves the other half that is\n925\tlost.\n926\t\n927\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n928\t\\section{Conclusion}\n929\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n930\tThis is just the beginning of the story.  Clearly a lot remains to be\n931\tdone to understand the nature of the Hawking\\index{Hawking effect}\n932\teffect in the setting of the thin-film domain\\index{domain wall} wall.\n933\tNevertheless, we hope that this analogue model will prove stimulating to\n934\tresearchers pondering the nature of Hawking\\index{Hawking effect}\n935\tradiation and information\\index{information loss} loss in\n936\tquantum\\index{quantum gravity} gravity on the one hand, and the\n937\tphysics of moving superfluid\\index{superfluid} textures\\index{texture}\n938\ton the other.\n939\t\n940\t\n941\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n942\t\\section*{Acknowledgments}\n943\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n944\tThe research described here is based partly on joint work by\n945\tG.~Volovik and TJ. We would like to thank G.~Volovik for helpful\n946\tdiscussions, and R.~Parentani for useful comments on a draft of this\n947\tarticle.  Most of this work was done while TK was visiting the Gravity\n948\tTheory Group at University of Maryland, for whose hospitality he is\n949\tvery grateful.  This research was supported in part by the Japan\n950\tSociety for the Promotion of Science and by the National Science\n951\tFoundation under NSF grant PHY-9800967.\n952\t\n953\t%---------------------------------------------------------------------\n954\t\\begin{thebibliography}{99}\n955\t%---------------------------------------------------------------------\n956\t\n957\t\\bibitem{TJcutoff}\n958\tT.~Jacobson,\n959\t``Black hole radiation in the presence \n960\tof a short distance cutoff'',\n961\tPhys.\\ Rev.\\ {\\bf D48}, 728 (1993)\n962\t[arXiv:hep-th/9303103].\n963\t%%CITATION = HEP-TH 9303103;%%\n964\t\n965\t\\bibitem{Ted-Unruh81}\n966\tW.G.~Unruh,\n967\t``Experimental black-hole evaporation?'',\n968\tPhys.\\ Rev.\\ Lett.\\ {\\bf 46}, 1351 (1981).\n969\t\n970\t\\bibitem{river}\n971\tT.~Jacobson,\n972\t``Trans--Planckian redshifts and the substance of the space-time river'',\n973\tProg.\\ Theor.\\ Phys.\\ Suppl.\\  {\\bf 136}, 1 (1999)\n974\t[arXiv:hep-th/0001085].\n975\t%%CITATION = HEP-TH 0001085;%%\n976\t\n977\t\\bibitem{CJsuper}\n978\tS.~Corley and T.~Jacobson,\n979\t``Black hole lasers'',\n980\tPhys.\\ Rev.\\ {\\bf D59}, 124011 (1999) [arXiv:hep-th/9806203].\n981\t%%CITATION = HEP-TH 9806203;%%\n982\t\n983\t\\bibitem{Anglin}\n984\tL.J.~Garay, J.~Anglin, J.I.~Cirac, and P.~Zoller,\n985\t``Black holes in Bose-Einstein condensates'',\n986\tPhys.\\ Rev.\\ Lett.\\  {\\bf 85}, 4643 (2000) [arXiv:gr-qc/0002015]; \n987\t%%CITATION = GR-QC 0002015;%%\n988\t``Sonic black holes in dilute Bose-Einstein condensates'',\n989\tPhys.\\ Rev.\\ A {\\bf 63}, 023611 (2001) [arXiv:gr-qc/0005131].\n990\t%%CITATION = GR-QC 0005131;%%\n991\t\n992\t\\bibitem{ultrashort}\n993\tT.~Jacobson,\n994\t``Black hole evaporation and ultrashort distances'',\n995\tPhys.\\ Rev.\\ {\\bf D44}, 1731 (1991).\n996\t%%CITATION = PHRVA,D44,1731;%%\n997\t\n998\t\\bibitem{TJorigin}\n999\tT.~Jacobson,\n1000\t``On the origin of the outgoing black hole modes'',\n1001\tPhys.\\ Rev.\\ {\\bf D53}, 7082 (1996)\n1002\t[arXiv:hep-th/9601064].\n1003\t%%CITATION = HEP-TH 9601064;%%\n1004\t\n1005\t\\bibitem{JVhorizons}\n1006\tT.A.~Jacobson and G.E.~Volovik,\n1007\t``Event horizons and ergoregions in He-3'',\n1008\tPhys.\\ Rev.\\ {\\bf D58}, 064021 (1998) [arXiv:cond-mat/9801308].\n1009\t%%CITATION = PHRVA,D58,064021;%%\n1010\t\n1011\t\\bibitem{KVdecay}\n1012\tN.B.~Kopnin and G.E.~Volovik,\n1013\t``Critical velocity and event horizon in \n1014\tpair-correlated systems with  `relativistic' \n1015\tfermionic quasiparticles'',\n1016\tPisma Zh.\\ Eksp.\\ Teor.\\ Fiz.\\ {\\bf 67}, 124 (1998)\n1017\t[arXiv:cond-mat/9712187].\n1018\t%%CITATION = COND-MAT 9712187;%%\n1019\t\n1020\t\\bibitem{JVfilm}\n1021\tT.A.~Jacobson and G.E.~Volovik,\n1022\t``Effective spacetime and Hawking radiation from \n1023\tmoving domain wall in  thin film of He-3-A'',\n1024\tPisma Zh.\\ Eksp.\\ Teor.\\ Fiz.\\ {\\bf 68}, 833 (1998)\n1025\t[JETP Lett. {\\bf 69}, 705 (1999)]\n1026\t[arXiv:gr-qc/9811014].\n1027\t%%CITATION = GR-QC 9811014;%%\n1028\t\n1029\t\\bibitem{Vtorus}\n1030\tG.E.~Volovik,\n1031\t``Simulation of Painlev\\'e--Gullstrand black hole \n1032\tin thin 3He-A film'',\n1033\tPisma Zh.\\ Eksp.\\ Teor.\\ Fiz.\\ {\\bf 69}, 662 (1999)\n1034\t[JETP Lett. {\\bf 69} 705 (1999)]\n1035\t[arXiv:gr-qc/9901077].\n1036\t%%CITATION = GR-QC 9901077;%%\n1037\t\n1038\t\\bibitem{VollWolf}\n1039\tD.~Vollhardt and P. W\\\"olfle, \n1040\t{\\it The Superfluid Phases of Helium 3}, (Taylor \\& Francis,\n1041\tLondon, 1990).\n1042\t\n1043\t\\bibitem{Vexotic}\n1044\tG.E.~Volovik, {\\it Exotic Properties of \n1045\tSuperfluid ${}^3$He}, (World Scientific, Singapore, 1992).\n1046\t\n1047\t\\bibitem{Leggett}\n1048\tA.~J.~Leggett, \n1049\t``A theoretical description of the new phases of liquid 3He'',\n1050\tRev.\\ Mod.\\ Phys.\\ {\\bf 47}, 331-414 (1975). \n1051\t\n1052\t\\bibitem{VolovikPR}G.E.~Volovik,\n1053\t``Superfluid analogies of cosmological phenomena'',\n1054\tPhys.\\ Rept.\\  {\\bf 351}, 195 (2001)\n1055\t[arXiv:gr-qc/0005091].\n1056\t%%CITATION = GR-QC 0005091;%%\n1057\t\n1058\t\\bibitem{HawkEllis}\n1059\tS.~W.~Hawking and G.~F.~R.~Ellis,\n1060\t{\\it The Large Scale Structure of Spacetime}, \n1061\t(Cambridge University Press, 1973).\n1062\t\n1063\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n1064\t\\end{thebibliography}\n1065\t%-------------------------------------------------------------------\n1066\t\n1067\t%------------------------------------------------------ \n1068\t\\end{document}\n1069\t%------------------------------------------------------\n1070\t"}]},"uuid":"3d2ade62-66e4-41e8-b5e6-1908acb46fe6","timestamp":"2026-08-15T19:38:58.190Z","sourceToolAssistantUUID":"845ee324-e31d-4633-b77b-051b6248d67a","userType":"external","entrypoint":"claude-desktop","cwd":"/Users/johnroehm/Programming/PythonEnvironments/Physics/Fluid-Based-Physics-Research/SK_EFT_Hawking","sessionId":"6cf37aa2-f1c7-4e33-a712-f17c2d75d99b","version":"2.1.229","gitBranch":"HEAD","slug":"swift-singing-llama"}
