{"parentUuid":"0fc91e85-1623-404d-907a-aba42607a210","isSidechain":true,"promptId":"d7b89794-41f0-46fe-9a20-6d198f8f624f","agentId":"a7a24c56a3aa309f4","type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_019LSpXxcXUr2U2Xb6Tc22Hj","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t\n2\t%\\documentstyle[preprint,aps]{revtex}\n3\t%\\documentstyle[preprint,eqsecnum,aps]{revtex}\n4\t%\\documentstyle[eqsecnum,aps]{revtex}\n5\t\n6\t\n7\t%\\documentstyle[aps,prb]{revtex}\n8\t%\\documentstyle[aps,prl,floats]{revtex}\n9\t%\\input epsf.def\n10\t\\documentstyle[aps,prl,floats,graphicx,epsfig]{revtex}\n11\t\n12\t\\begin{document}\n13\t\\draft\n14\t\n15\t\\twocolumn[\\hsize\\textwidth\\columnwidth\\hsize\\csname @twocolumnfalse\\endcsname\n16\t\n17\t\n18\t\\title{ Event horizons and ergoregions in\n19\t$^3$He }\n20\t\\author{ T.A. Jacobson$^{1}$ and G.E. Volovik$^{2,3}$}\n21\t\\address{\n22\t$^{1}$Department of Physics, University of\n23\tMaryland\\\\ College Park, MD 20742-4111, USA\\\\\n24\t$^{2}$Low Temperature Laboratory, Helsinki University of\n25\tTechnology\\\\\n26\tP.O.Box 2200, FIN-02015 HUT, Finland\\\\\n27\t$^{3}$L.D. Landau Institute for\n28\tTheoretical Physics, \\\\ Kosygin Str. 2, 117940 Moscow, Russia }\n29\t\n30\t\n31\t\\date{\\today}\n32\t\\maketitle\n33\t\n34\t\n35\t\\begin{abstract}\n36\tEvent horizons  for fermion quasiparticles naturally arise in\n37\tmoving textures in superconductors and Fermi superfluids. We discuss\n38\tthe example of a planar soliton moving in superfluid $^3$He-A,\n39\twhich is closely analogous to a charged rotating black hole.\n40\tThe moving soliton will radiate quasiparticles via the Hawking effect\n41\tat a temperature of about 5 $\\mu$K, and via vacuum polarization\n42\tinduced by the effective `electromagnetic field'\n43\tand `ergoregion'.  Superfluid $^3$He-A thus appears to be a useful system\n44\tfor experimental and theoretical simulations of quantum effects\n45\trelated to event horizons and ergoregions.\\end{abstract}\n46\t\n47\t\\\n48\t\n49\t\\pacs{PACS numbers: 04.70.Dy, 65.57.-z, 67.57.Fg}\n50\t\n51\t\\\n52\t\n53\t] \\narrowtext\n54\t%\\twocolumn\n55\t\n56\t\\section{ Introduction}.\n57\t\n58\tA black hole event horizon is the causal boundary of the exterior\n59\tregion of spacetime.\n60\tAccording to quantum mechanics,\n61\tan event horizon emits Hawking\n62\tradiation\\cite{Hawking} and possesses a Bekenstein\n63\tentropy\\cite{Bekenstein}. These phenomena lie at the\n64\tintersection of gravity and quantum mechanics, and have\n65\tplayed a major role in efforts to understand quantum gravity.\n66\tHowever, the nature of the fundamental degrees of freedom and the\n67\tphysics at short distances is still not understood,\n68\tso basic questions about the statistical\n69\tmeaning of black hole entropy, the back-reaction to Hawking radiation,\n70\tthe origin of the outgoing modes, and unitarity, remain\n71\tunresolved. Moreover, the effect of the Hawking radiation is\n72\tnegligible\n73\tfor the physics of solar mass black holes,\n74\tsince the temperature of the\n75\tHawking radiation $T_H$ is extremely small ($\\sim 10^{-7}$ K).\n76\tThe only conceivable experimental consequences of the Hawking\n77\tradiation at present would arise from evaporation of a (hypothetical)\n78\tpopulation of primordial black holes.\n79\t\n80\tFor this reason models simulating\n81\tevent horizons in condensed matter can be useful.\n82\tThe first attempt at a model of this kind was made with a  moving\n83\tliquid \\cite{UnruhSonic,Jacobson1991,Visser1997}. The propagation of\n84\tsound\n85\twaves on the background of a moving inhomogeneous liquid is similar to the\n86\tpropagation of light in (3+1)-dimensional Lorentzian geometry, and is governed\n87\tby the relativistic wave equation:\n88\t$$\\partial_\\mu\\left(\\sqrt{-g}g^{\\mu\\nu}\\partial_\\nu\\Psi\\right)=0~~.\\eqno(1.1)$$\n89\tThe `acoustic'  metric $g^{\\mu\\nu}$, in which the sound wave is\n90\tpropagating, is determined by the inhomogeneity and local flow velocity of the\n91\tliquid.  If the liquid moves supersonically a sonic `event horizon' can\n92\tarise. A drawback of this model for the simulation of black hole\n93\tphysics\n94\tis that ordinary liquids are essentially dissipative systems and are\n95\tvery far from the\n96\tcondition where quantum effects can be of any importance: this smears the\n97\teffects that, like the Hawking effect, are related to quantum fluctuations.\n98\t\n99\tBetter candidates are superfluids, which allow\n100\tnondissipative  motion of the vacuum (superfluid condensate,\n101\tor ground state), and which also support well defined elementary excitations\n102\tthat propagate in a `curved space' of the inhomogeneous moving condensate.\n103\tThe Fermi superfluids (including superconductors) are appealing\n104\tcandidates because their\n105\tlow temperature dynamics are described by quantum field theories similar to\n106\tthose in high energy physics\\cite{Wilczek}.\n107\tAmong them superfluid $^3$He-A has the\n108\tadvantage that this superfluid supports an effective gravity caused by some\n109\tcomponents of the superfluid order\n110\tparameter\\cite{Exotic}.\n111\t\n112\tThere is one important obstacle to the formation of an horizon in a\n113\tmoving condensate: superfluidity collapses, i.e. the condensate\n114\tdisappears, before the corresponding speed of light is reached. For example in\n115\tsuperfluid $^4$He the Landau velocity at which the  condensate is\n116\tunstable to roton excitation is smaller than the speed of sound and\n117\tthus the supersonic flow can not be established. For\n118\tfermionic systems the collapse of  superfluid/superconducting state due to\n119\t``superluminal\" motion of the condensate was discussed in\n120\t\\cite{KopninVolovik1998a}.\n121\tTherefore we have looked for a model in\n122\twhich the condensate is at rest with respect to the  container.\n123\t\n124\tWe show here that a `superluminally' moving inhomogeneity of the order\n125\tparameter (soliton, vortex or other texture) in superfluid $^3$He-A  provides\n126\tsuch a model and can simulate the physics of\n127\tan event horizon and ergoregion for `relativistic'\n128\tmassless fermions---the Bogoliubov-Nambu  quasiparticles. The\n129\t`superluminally' moving soliton produces dissipation due to quantum\n130\tradiation of the fermions via several mechanisms, which decreases  the\n131\tsoliton velocity. Similar processes\n132\toccur also for a charged, rotating, black hole, where the\n133\tSchwinger pair production, pair production in the ergoregion outside\n134\tthe horizon, and Hawking radiation lead to discharge, spin-down, and\n135\tevaporation of the black hole. So both the `superluminally' moving soliton and\n136\tthe black hole are quasi-equilibrium, unstable inhomogeneous states\n137\texhibiting an event\n138\thorizon.\n139\t\n140\t\n141\t\\section{ Relativistic fermions in $^3$He-A.}\n142\t\n143\t\n144\tThe spontaneous breaking of symmetry in the superfluid condensate in $^3$He-A\n145\tis characterized in part by a unit vector $\\hat l$, which\n146\tpoints along the spontaneous angular momentum of the Cooper pairs and\n147\tdetermines\n148\tthe direction of the zeroes in the energy spectrum of the\n149\tBogoliubov-Nambu fermion quasiparticles \\cite{Vollhardt1990,Exotic}\n150\t$$E(\\vec p)=\\pm\\sqrt{ v_F^2(p-p_F)^2 +{\\Delta_A^2\\over p_F^2}(\\hat\n151\tl \\times\\vec p)^2}~~.\\eqno(2.1)$$\n152\tHere $v_F(p-p_F)$ is the quasiparticle energy in the normal Fermi liquid above\n153\ttransition, with $p_F$ the Fermi momentum and $v_F=p_F/m^*$; $m^*$ is the\n154\teffective mass, which is of order the mass $m_3$ of the $^3$He atom;\n155\t$\\Delta_A$ is the so-called gap amplitude.\n156\t\n157\tThe energy in Eq.(2.1) is zero at two points $\\vec p\n158\t= e \\vec A$ with $\\vec A= p_F\\hat l$ and $e=\\pm 1$. Close to the two zeroes\n159\tof the energy spectrum one can expand in $\\vec p\n160\t- e \\vec A$ and the spectrum $E(\\vec p)$  becomes\n161\tthat of a charged, massless relativistic particle propagating\n162\tin a curved spacetime in the presence of an electromagnetic vector\n163\tpotential:\n164\t$$ g^{\\mu\\nu}(p_\\mu -eA_\\mu) (p_\\nu -eA_\\nu)=0~~.\\eqno(2.2)$$\n165\tThe `four-momentum' $p_\\mu$, `electromagnetic vector potential' $A_\\mu$,\n166\tand inverse `metric tensor' $g^{\\mu\\nu}$ in this covariant expression\n167\tare specified by giving their components in the coordinate system\n168\t$(x^0,x^i)$ where $x^0$ is the Newtonian time $t$ and $x^i=$\n169\tare Cartesian spatial coordinates\n170\tat rest with respect to the superfluid:\n171\t$$(p_0,\\; p_i)=(-E,\\;  p_i),\\eqno(2.3a)$$\n172\t$$(A_0,\\; A_i)=(0,\\;  p_F  l_i),\\eqno(2.3b)$$\n173\t$$g^{00}=-1,~~~~g^{0i}=0,~~~~\n174\tg^{ik}= c_\\perp^2 (\\delta^{ik} -   l^i  l^k) +  c_\\parallel^2   l^i\n175\t l^k ~~.~~ \\eqno(2.3c)$$\n176\t$E$ and $p_i$ on the right hand side of (2.3a) are the\n177\tNewtonian energy and momentum, and the index on $p_i$ and $l_i$ on the\n178\tright hand sides of (2.3a) and (2.3b) is lowered with the Euclidian metric\n179\t$\\delta_{ij}$.  (Once the ``relativistic\" quantities are defined by (2.3),\n180\tthe Euclidean metric plays no further explicit role in the dynamics.)\n181\tThe fermion quasiparticles actually satisfy the curved\n182\tspacetime  Weyl equation for massless charged chiral\n183\tspinors\\cite{Exotic,Volovik1986},\n184\talthough for our purposes here all that is needed is the dispersion\n185\trelation (2.2). In general there is an additional term in the vector\n186\tpotential\\cite{Volovik1986}\n187\twhich is proportional to the gradient of the $\\hat l$ vector.\n188\tAlso, the square of the Weyl equation contains extra terms: in symbolic\n189\tform it is of the type   $(p-eA)^2 + R + \\sigma\\cdot F =0$. Here $R$ is the\n190\tRicci scalar, $F$ is the electromagnetic field strength,\n191\tand $\\sigma$ is the spin (in our case it is the\n192\tBogoliubov-Nambu ``spin\" of quasiparticles in particle-hole space).\n193\tWe ignore all these extra terms in the dispersion relation (2.2),\n194\tsince they are proportional to the gradients of the $\\hat l$ vector\n195\tand thus are small in the $\\hat l$ texture discussed here:\n196\t$F \\propto \\nabla \\hat l$, $R \\propto (\\nabla \\hat\n197\tl)^2$. In principle  these terms affect the propagation of the field,\n198\thowever they play no essential role in the particle production processes\n199\tstudied here.\n200\tHereafter we omit the quotes when referring to the quasi gravitational and\n201\telectromagnetic fields, since no actual such fields  enter our problem.\n202\t\n203\tThe quantities $c_\\perp= \\Delta_A / p_F$  and $c_\\parallel=v_F$\n204\tin the inverse metric (2.3c) are `speeds of light'\n205\tpropagating transverse to $\\hat l$ and along $\\hat l$ correspondingly.\n206\tThe magnitudes of the $^3$He-A parameters at zero pressure are:\n207\t$m^*\\simeq 3m_{\\rm He-3}$, $\\Delta_A\\simeq 1.7 {\\rm mK}$, $v_F\\simeq 55 {\\rm\n208\tm/s}$, $\\Delta_A / p_F \\simeq 3 {\\rm\n209\tcm/s}$. As a result the `speed  of light' is very anisotropic\n210\t(in Cartesian coordinates):\n211\t$c_\\perp\\simeq 0.5\\cdot10^{-3} c_\\parallel $.\n212\tThe relativistic approximation (2.2) is valid provided $p-p_F\\ll p_F$\n213\tand $p_\\perp=|\\vec p\\times\\hat l| \\ll m^*c_\\perp$. The condition\n214\t$E\\ll m^*c_\\perp^2\\sim 0.5\\cdot 10^{-3}T_c \\sim  0.5\\mu$K\n215\tis thus sufficient for this approximation.\n216\tThis upper limit is still significantly  lower than the lowest\n217\tconfirmed temperature reached so far in superfluid $^3$He experiments,\n218\tabout $100\\mu$K. The actual lower bound is probably lower than\n219\tthis but at the moment there is\n220\tno reliable thermometry below $100\\mu$K \\cite{Bunkov}.\n221\tIf the energy is  higher than $m^*c_\\perp^2$, `non-relativistic'\n222\thigher order corrections must be added in general.\n223\tHowever there are many examples (such\n224\tas axial anomaly and zero charge effect) where only\n225\tthe propagation along the $\\hat l$-axis\n226\tis important, in which case the only restriction is that $T\\ll\n227\tT_c$ so that the thermal fermions are concentrated in the\n228\tvicinity of the nodes.\n229\t\n230\tIf the $\\hat l$ texture moves with constant velocity\n231\t$\\vec v$, then to obtain manifest time-independence of the\n232\tbackground one must use\n233\tthe coordinate system which is at rest with respect to the texture.\n234\tLet us from now\n235\ton  denote the coordinates in the texture frame by the unprimed\n236\tletters $(t,x^i)$, and those\n237\tin the superfluid frame by the primed letters\n238\t$(t',x'^i)=(t,x^i+v^i t)$, where $v^i$ is the velocity of the texture.\n239\tThe dispersion relation\n240\tin the moving frame is obtained from (2.2) and (2.3a,b,c)\n241\tsimply by finding the\n242\tcomponents of the tensors $p_\\mu$, $A_\\mu$, and $g^{\\mu\\nu}$ in the\n243\tnew coordinate system\\footnote{We use here the fact that, under the\n244\tGalilean transformation of coordinates,\n245\tthe tensor transformation law for the covariant ({\\it not} contravariant)\n246\t4-momentum agrees with the Galilean transformation law for the\n247\tenergy and momentum of quasiparticles, so the resulting components\n248\tof $p_\\mu'$ are in fact the correct Galilean components. That is,\n249\tit is not necessary to transform back to the rest frame of the\n250\tsuperfluid in order to correctly identify the Galilean energy and momentum.}:\n251\t$$(p_0,\\; p_i)=(-E'+p'_iv^i,\\; p'_i),\\eqno(2.4a)$$\n252\t$$(A_0,\\; A_i)=(p_F l_iv^i,\\; p_F l_i),\\eqno(2.4b)$$\n253\t$$g^{00}=-1,~~~~g^{0i}=v^i,~~~~\n254\tg^{ik}= c_\\perp^2 (\\delta^{ik} -   l^i  l^k) +  c_\\parallel^2   l^i\n255\t l^k -v^iv^k~~.~~ \\eqno(2.4c)$$\n256\tNote that $-p_0=E=E'-p'_i v^i$ is just the energy $E$\n257\tof the quasiparticle in the moving frame.  In the moving frame the\n258\tmetric tensor, and electromagnetic vector potential do not depend on time and\n259\tthus the quasiparticle energy $E$ is {\\em conserved}.\n260\tThe condition $|E'|\\ll m^*c_\\perp^2$ which ensures the\n261\tvalidity of the  relativistic approximation\n262\tbecomes, in terms of $E$, $|E+p_iv^i|\\ll m^*c_\\perp^2$.\n263\t\n264\t\\section{ Moving soliton.}\n265\t\n266\t\n267\tAccording to Eq.(2.2) the low-energy fermions move in gravitational and\n268\telectromagnetic fields simulated by\n269\tthe $\\hat l$ texture and its   velocity  $\\vec v$.\n270\tAs explained above, to avoid the collapse of the condensate it is important to\n271\thave the superfluid at rest with respect to the container, so we do not\n272\tintroduce\n273\tthe  velocity field $\\vec v_s$. While the superflow is limited by the\n274\tcritical velocity $\\sim c_\\perp$\n275\tabove which the $^3$He-A phase\n276\tis destroyed and the broken symmetry is restored, the velocity\n277\t$v$ of the texture can  exceed $ c_\\perp$ and can approach $v_F$\n278\t\\cite{LeggettYip,Schopohl}. The $\\hat l$-solitons are\n279\twell resolved in NMR experiments \\cite{VortexSheetExp}, and pulsed NMR\n280\tcan be used to accelerate them.\n281\t\n282\tHere we consider a topologically stable texture, a ``domain wall\" soliton\n283\tmoving with velocity $v$ in the $z$ direction. We choose the so-called splay\n284\tsoliton\\cite{Vollhardt1990}\n285\t$$\\hat l= \\hat z \\cos \\alpha(z) +  \\hat x \\sin \\alpha(z)~~,~~z= z'-vt\n286\t~~,\\eqno(3.1)$$ where $z$ is the coordinate co-moving with the soliton and\n287\t$z'$ is the coordinate in the superfluid frame. Since the exact structure of\n288\tthe realistic soliton\\cite{Vollhardt1990}\n289\tis not important for our purposes,  we consider a\n290\tsimplified profile for this soliton,\n291\t$$\\hat l= -\\hat z\\;\n292\t\\tanh{z\\over d}  +  \\hat x\\; \\mbox{sech}\\,\n293\t{z\\over d}~~.\\eqno(3.2)$$\n294\tThe thickness $d$ of the\n295\tsoliton is on the order of the so-called dipole length\n296\t$\\xi_D\\sim 10~\\mu$. The profile of the soliton is shown in\n297\tFig. 1.\n298\t\n299\t%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%\n300\t\\begin{figure}[!!!t]\n301\t%\\centerline{\\epsfxsize=0.40\\textwidth\\epsfbox{SolitonFig1.eps}}\n302\t%\\bigskip\n303\t\\begin{center}\n304\t\\leavevmode\n305\t\\epsfig{file=SolitonFig1.eps,width=0.8\\linewidth}\n306\t\\caption[soliton1]\n307\t    {Profile of the $z$-projection of the vector $\\vec l$ across the\n308\t splay soliton wall in superfluid $^3$He-A.\n309\t  This soliton is topologically stable and can\n310\t  propagate in the liquid without destruction.}\n311\t\\label{soliton1}\n312\t\\end{center}\n313\t\\end{figure}\n314\t%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%\n315\t\n316\tThe vector potential and metric tensor in the frame comoving with the soliton\n317\tdo not depend on time, nor do they depend on the $x$ or $y$ coordinates.\n318\tThus the energy $E=-p_0$ and momentum components $p_x$ and $p_y$ of the\n319\tfermions\n320\tare conserved quantities. The equations (2.4) and (3.1) give the following\n321\tnonzero components for the vector potential:\n322\t$$A_0=vp_F\\cos\\alpha,~~~~A_x=p_F\\sin\\alpha,~~~~A_z=p_F\\cos\\alpha~,\\eqno(3.3)$$\n323\tand for the inverse metric:\n324\t$$g^{00}=-1,~~~~g^{0z}=v,~~~~g^{yy}=c_\\perp^2,\n325\t$$\n326\t$$g^{zz}=c_\\perp^2\\sin^2\\alpha +v_F^2\\cos^2\\alpha -v^2~,~ $$\n327\t$$g^{xx}= c_\\perp^2 \\cos^2\\alpha +v_F^2\n328\t\\sin^2\\alpha,~~~~g^{zx}=(v_F^2- c_\\perp^2) \\sin \\alpha  \\cos \\alpha~.~\n329\t\\eqno(3.4)$$\n330\t\n331\t\\section{ Pair production in electromagnetic field.}\n332\t\n333\tThe vector potential associated with the moving\n334\tsoliton gives rise to both magnetic and electric fields. In the\n335\tsoliton frame the electromagnetic field strength tensor\n336\t$F_{\\mu\\nu}=\\partial_\\mu A_\\nu-\\partial_\\nu A_\\mu$ has the nonzero\n337\tcomponents\n338\t$$F_{zx}=p_F \\partial_z\\sin\\alpha,\n339\t~~~~F_{0z}=vp_F \\partial_z\\cos\\alpha~.\\eqno(4.1)$$\n340\tThe invariant combination\n341\t$$``{\\bf B}^2-{\\bf E}^2~\"={1\\over\n342\t2}F_{\\mu\\nu}F_{\\alpha\\beta}g^{\\mu\\alpha}g^{\\nu\\beta}= v_F^2c_\\perp^2\n343\tF_{zx}^2\\left(1 -{v^2\\over v_F^2\\cos^2\\alpha}\\right)~~\\eqno(4.3)$$ does not\n344\tdepend on the coordinate frame. For any velocity $v$ there are two planes\n345\t$z=\\pm\n346\tz_p$,\n347\t$$\\cos^2\\alpha(z_p)= {v^2\\over v_F^2} ~~, \\eqno(4.4)$$\n348\twhere the magnitude of the electric field equals the\n349\tmagnitude of the magnetic field. In the region between these planes, where\n350\t${\\bf E}^2>{\\bf B}^2$, the electric field induces the Schwinger production of\n351\tpairs of fermions \\cite{Schwinger}. This leads to dissipation during the motion\n352\tof the soliton, which gives rise to a friction force on the soliton even at\n353\tzero\n354\ttemperature and the soliton will decelerate.\n355\t\n356\tFor textures where\n357\t$A_0(z)$ has equal asymptotes $A_0(\\infty)=A_0(-\\infty)$ at both\n358\tinfinities the\n359\tsituation is different. In this case the  potential $ \\Phi(z)=A_0(z)- A_0(\\pm\n360\t\\infty)$ represents a potential well for the fermions. The\n361\tfermions formed by Schwinger radiation finally occupy all the negative energy\n362\tstates in this potential well. After that the radiation stops. The filling of\n363\tthe negative energy levels will lead to a modification of the vacuum in the\n364\tvicinity of the soliton.  After that the soliton with the modified structure\n365\twill move without friction. In our case the potential well is unbounded,\n366\t$A_0(\\infty)=-A_0(-\\infty)\\neq A_0(-\\infty)$. The negative energy levels cannot\n367\tbe filled, thus the radiation will lead to the deceleration of the soliton\n368\tuntil\n369\tit reaches zero velocity.\n370\t\n371\t\\section{ Horizon and ergoregion for the fermions.}\n372\t\n373\t\n374\tIf the velocity $v$ of the soliton exceeds $c_\\perp$, the metric (3.4)\n375\tdescribes a\n376\tplanar ``black hole\" with an ergoregion outside the horizon, or rather a black\n377\thole/white hole pair. In the frame of the soliton,\n378\tthe horizons are lightlike surfaces at fixed position $z=\\pm z_h$. These\n379\tare given by an equation $f(z)=0$, where\n380\tthe gradient $\\partial_\\mu f$ is lightlike:\n381\t$0=g^{\\mu\\nu}\\partial_\\mu f\\partial_\\nu f=g^{zz}(\\partial_z f)^2$.\n382\tThat is, at the horizons one has $g^{zz}=0$, or\n383\t$$c_\\perp^2\n384\t\\sin^2\\alpha(z) +v_F^2\n385\t\\cos^2\\alpha(z) =v^2~~. \\eqno(5.1)$$\n386\tThus\n387\t$$\\cos^2\\alpha(z_h)=\\frac{v^2-c_\\perp^2}{v_F^2-c_\\perp^2}~.\\eqno(5.2)$$\n388\t\n389\tThe physical meaning of these horizons is revealed if one\n390\tintroduces $c^{z}$, the `speed of light in the $z$ direction' in\n391\tthe superfluid rest frame. Any\n392\tplanar lightlike surface (``wavefront\") is given by an equation $f(t,z')=0$,\n393\twhere $z'=z+vt$  is the coordinate in the superfluid frame, and\n394\t$c^{z}$ is defined by  $(\\partial_t  +c^z\\partial_{z'}) f=0$.\n395\tThe lightlike condition on the gradient $\\partial_\\mu f$\n396\tyields $c^{z}=(g'^{z'z'})^{1/2}$. Since\n397\t$g'^{z'z'}=g^{zz} + v^2$, the horizons (at $g^{zz}=0$ in Eq.(5.2)) occur where\n398\tthe speed of light equals the velocity of the soliton, $c^{z}(z_h)=v$. The\n399\tspeed of particles from the region between the horizons is less than $v$\n400\tin the $z$-direction\n401\tand thus they cannot propagate out across the leading horizon. Furthermore no\n402\tquasiparticle can enter the trailing horizon from the left because as\n403\tit approaches its speed drops to the speed of the soliton. So the leading\n404\t(future) event horizon  is the black hole and the trailing (past) event\n405\thorizon is the white hole (Fig.2).\n406\t\n407\tThe horizons appear in the\n408\tmoving soliton if $v>c_\\perp$.\n409\tNote that the ${\\bf E}^2>{\\bf B}^2$ region (4.4)\n410\textends a bit outside the horizon, and exists even when $v<c_\\perp$\n411\tand there is no horizon.\n412\t\n413\t%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%\n414\t\\begin{figure}[!!!t]\n415\t%\\centerline{\\epsfxsize=0.40\\textwidth\\epsfbox{SolitonFig2.eps}}\n416\t%\\bigskip\n417\t\\begin{center}\n418\t\\leavevmode\n419\t\\epsfig{file=SolitonFig2.eps,width=0.8\\linewidth}\n420\t\\caption[soliton2]\n421\t    {The ``speed of light\" in the $z$-direction in the superfluid frame,\n422\t$c^z(z)$.\n423\t Quasiparticles in the region $-z_h<z<z_h$, where the speed of light is less\n424\t than the velocity $v$ of the soliton, cannot propagate to the right in the\n425\t frame of the moving texture (the arrows show\n426\t the possible directions of quasiparticle motion in the $z$-direction).\n427\t This region is bounded by the black and white hole horizons. }\n428\t\\label{soliton2}\n429\t\\end{center}\n430\t\\end{figure}\n431\t%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%\n432\t\n433\tThe ``ergoregion\" is the region where a particle must go faster than\n434\tlight in order to remain at the same value of $(x,y,z)$. This occurs\n435\twhere $g_{tt}>0$. In the ergoregion the time translation Killing field\n436\t$\\partial_t$ is {\\em spacelike}, so the conserved ``energy\" can be\n437\tnegative even for a future pointing timelike\n438\tfour-momentum. As a result the vacuum in the ergoregion is unstable\n439\tto creation of pairs of particles, both with future pointing momenta,\n440\twith total energy zero. Put differently, the conserved ``energy\"  can\n441\tbe {\\it positive} even for a {\\it past} pointing\n442\ttimelike four-momentum. For $^3$He this means that a state in the\n443\toccupied valence band (i.e. with the negative sign of the square root in\n444\tEq.(2.1)) has positive energy and thus can tunnel out away from the\n445\tergoregion, leaving behind a negative energy hole state.\n446\t\n447\tThe ergoplanes---boundaries of the ergoregion---occur at\n448\t$z=\\pm z_e$ where $g_{tt}=0$,\n449\twhich yields\n450\t$$\\cos^2\\alpha(z_e)=\n451\t\\frac{1-c_\\perp^2/v^2}{1-c_\\perp^2/v_F^2}~.\\eqno(5.3)$$\n452\tAn ergoregion exists for this soliton only if $v>c_\\perp$,\n453\tso there is an ergoregion if and only if there is an event horizon.\n454\tThe ergoplanes lie outside the event horizons (5.2) and outside\n455\tthe Schwinger pair region (4.4) unless $v$ is extremely close to $c_\\perp$\n456\t(i.e. unless $v<c_\\perp(1-c_\\perp^2/v_F^2)^{-1/2}$).\n457\t\n458\tThe locations of the boundary of the Schwinger pair production region $z_p$,\n459\tevent horizon $z_h$, and ergoplane $z_e$ depend on the velocity $v$\n460\tof the soliton. To get an idea of these locations and their scale\n461\twe have plotted in Fig. 3 the coordinate $z$ versus\n462\t$\\log(v/c_\\perp)$  for each of these three positions.\n463\tThe Fermi velocity is at the abscissa $\\sim 3$\n464\t($v_F/c_\\perp\\sim 10^3$).\n465\tRecall that $d\\sim 10^5 \\AA$, so Fig. 3 shows that\n466\t$z_h$ is smaller than $10^3 \\AA$ until\n467\t$v\\sim 10 c_\\perp$.\n468\t\n469\t\n470\t%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%\n471\t\\begin{figure}[!!!t]\n472\t%\\centerline{\\epsfxsize=0.40\\textwidth\\epsfbox{SolitonFig3.eps}}\n473\t%\\bigskip\n474\t\\begin{center}\n475\t\\leavevmode\n476\t\\epsfig{file=SolitonFig3.eps,width=0.8\\linewidth}\n477\t\\caption[soliton3]\n478\t    {Locations of the horizons, the ergoplanes and the boundaries of the region\n479\t  of pair production by the electric field, as a function of the velocity $v$\n480\t  of the soliton.}\n481\t\\label{soliton3}\n482\t\\end{center}\n483\t\\end{figure}\n484\t%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%\n485\t\n486\t\n487\tThe horizon has a `transverse velocity' because\n488\tthe light rays on the horizon are actually moving in the $x$ direction.\n489\tThis is because the $\\hat l$ vector has an $x$-component, so the\n490\tspeed of light is faster in the $x$-direction on the\n491\thorizon. This is analogous to the rotational\n492\tvelocity of the horizon of a rotating black hole.\n493\tTo compute this velocity it is helpful to introduce the\n494\t``horizon generating Killing field\" $\\chi^\\mu$, which is tangent to the\n495\tlightlike curves that generate the horizon.\n496\tSince it is spacelike on the horizon, the vector field $\\partial_t$\n497\tis clearly {\\it not} the horizon generating Killing field.\n498\tRather, we have\n499\t$$\n500\t\\chi=\\partial_t + w\\partial_x ~~,\n501\t\\eqno(5.4)\n502\t$$\n503\twhere $w$ is some constant which we call the {\\it transverse\n504\tvelocity} of the horizon. Since the horizon is a lightlike surface,\n505\t$\\chi$ must be orthogonal to $\\partial_x$, so\n506\t$0=g_{\\mu\\nu}\\chi^\\mu(\\partial_x)^\\nu=g_{tx}+wg_{xx}$.\n507\tThus $w=-(g_{tx}/g_{xx})_h=(g^{zx})_h/v$, or\n508\t$$\n509\tw=v_F\\sqrt{\\frac{1-v^2/v_F^2}{1-c_\\perp^2/ v^2}}~~.\n510\t\\eqno(5.5)\n511\t$$\n512\tA lightlike surface generated by a Killing field is called a\n513\t{\\it Killing horizon}, so our black hole\n514\thorizon is a Killing horizon.\n515\tThe surface gravity $\\kappa$ of a Killing horizon can be\n516\tdefined by the equation $\\partial_a(\\chi^2)=-2\\kappa\\chi_a$,\n517\tevaluated on the horizon. Direct but tedious\n518\tcomputation yields\n519\t$$\n520\t\\kappa=\\frac{dg^{zz}/dz}{2v}\\vert_h =(dc^z/dz)\\vert_h\n521\t~~,\\eqno(5.6)\n522\t$$\n523\tor\n524\t$$\n525\t\\kappa=\\frac{v_F}{d}(1-\\frac{v^2}{v_F^2})\n526\t\\sqrt{\\frac{1-c_\\perp^2/v^2}{1-c_\\perp^2/ v_F^2}}~~.\\eqno(5.7)\n527\t$$\n528\t\n529\t\n530\t\\section{ Hawking radiation.}\n531\t\n532\t\n533\tThe Hawking temperature\n534\tis determined by the surface gravity as\n535\t$$T_H={\\hbar\\over 2\\pi k_B} \\kappa ~~,\\eqno(6.1)$$\n536\twhere $\\kappa$ is given by Eq.(5.6) or (5.7).   Note that, as in\n537\tthe case of Unruh's sonic black hole model, the Hawking temperature\n538\tis given by the gradient of a velocity at the horizon. However, in the sonic\n539\tcase it was the velocity of the fluid, whereas in the present case it is\n540\tthe (anisotropic) velocity of the fermion quasiparticles.\n541\tAs long as the soliton velocity $v$ is not too close to either $v_F$\n542\tor $c_\\perp$,  then $\\kappa \\simeq v_F/d$, which gives\n543\t$T_H\\simeq 5\\mu$K. This is  an order of magnitude lower than\n544\tthe lowest confirmed temperature reached in\n545\tsuperfluid $^3$He experiments today, but is\n546\tan order of magnitude higher than the temperature\n547\t$\\simeq 0.5\\mu$K above which the nonrelativistic corrections become\n548\timportant.\n549\t\n550\t\n551\tThe Hawking flux for fermions has the form\\cite{Hawking}\n552\t$$\\Gamma\\, \\Bigl[\\exp\\Bigl((E-\\mu)/k_BT_H\\Bigr)+1\\Bigr]^{-1}\n553\t\\eqno(6.2),$$\n554\twhere $\\Gamma$ and $\\mu$\n555\tare the emission coefficient and ``chemical potential\" for the mode\n556\tin question.\n557\tIn our case, $\\mu$ is given by\n558\t$$\\mu= p_x w  + e A_0(z_h)\\eqno(6.3)$$\n559\t(neglecting the spin energy), where $w$ is the transverse velocity\n560\tof the horizon (5.5) and $A_0(z_h)$ is the scalar potential (3.3)\n561\tevaluated at the event horizon.\n562\tBy way of analogy, for a rotating charged black\n563\thole one has\n564\t$\\mu= J \\Omega + e\\Phi$ where $J$ and $e$ are the the angular momentum\n565\tand charge of the mode, and\n566\t$\\Omega$ and $\\Phi$ are the angular velocity and the\n567\telectric potential of the horizon.\n568\tThe quantity $E$ in (6.2) is $-p_0$, the conserved energy in\n569\tthe comoving frame of the soliton, which according to (2.4a)\n570\tis equal to $E'-p'_z v$ where $E'$ and $p'_z(=p_z)$ are the energy\n571\tand momentum in the frame of the superfluid.\n572\tWe remind the reader that there is a constraint\n573\t$\\vert E'\\vert \\ll m^*c_\\perp^2$ on the quasiparticle energy\n574\tin order for the relativistic description to be\n575\tgenerally valid. In terms of $E$ this constraint becomes\n576\t$|E+p_z v|\\ll m^*c_\\perp^2$. Since $p_z$ is not conserved\n577\tthis condition may be satisfied at one point of a quasiparticle\n578\ttrajectory and not at another. A complete analysis of the\n579\tparticle creation processes will therefore require the nonrelativistic\n580\ttreatment in general, although the extent of the nonrelativisitic\n581\tcorrections will depend on the type of texture and other parameters\n582\tof the system.\n583\t\n584\tThe existence of Hawking radiation in the black hole case follows from\n585\tthe assumption that near the horizon the high frequency\n586\toutgoing modes of the quantum field  are in the\n587\tground state as defined in a frame falling freely across the horizon.\n588\tWhen the temperature of the heat bath  (normal component of the liquid) is very\n589\tlow, this assumption holds  for the moving soliton in $^3$He, since the\n590\t``freely\n591\tfalling frame\" is the  frame of the superfluid which is at rest with respect to\n592\tthe container (and thus to the heat bath). The passage of the moving texture\n593\tthrough this frame is essentially adiabatic for the high frequency modes.\n594\tAs a\n595\tresult, the distribution of the fermions in the soliton frame\n596\tremains thermal and is given by the\n597\tfermi-function\n598\t$f(E')$ with $E'=E-\\vec p\\cdot\\vec v_n$, where $\\vec v_n$ is the velocity\n599\tof the\n600\theat bath; and $E$ and $\\vec{p}$ are in the soliton frame.\n601\t\n602\tThe vacuum is therefore not excited directly by any time dependent forcing,\n603\tbut it is unstable to tunneling processes arising from both `level crossing'\n604\tand the Hawking effect. The level crossing leads to Schwinger pair production\n605\tin the `electric' field, as well as pair production in the ergoregion\n606\tthat would occur even in the absence of electric charge in analogy with\n607\tthe process outside a rotating black hole. What happens is that the\n608\tFermi sea is `tilted' in space, and some states under the Fermi surface\n609\tnear the soliton have positive energy relative to the Fermi surface\n610\tfar from the soliton. Quasiparticles in these states may tunnel out\n611\tleaving behind quasiholes (or {\\it vice versa}) that are swept past the\n612\thorizon.\n613\t\n614\tIt was realized\\cite{levelxing} shortly after Hawking's discovery\n615\tthat the flux from pair creation due to level crossing outside the horizon\n616\tcorresponds to the contribution from states with $E<\\mu$ in the\n617\tflux formula (6.2). As $T_H\\rightarrow0$, the flux is\n618\textinguished for states with $E>\\mu$, whereas for states with $E<\\mu$\n619\tit approaches the nonzero value $\\Gamma$, the tunneling probability.\n620\tAt finite Hawking temperature the flux is modified as indicated by (6.2).\n621\t\n622\tTo determine the actual magnitude of the Hawking flux\n623\tand ``level crossing flux\"\n624\tit is necessary to\n625\tevaluate the  emission\n626\tcoefficients (or so-called ``grey-body factors\")\n627\t$\\Gamma(E,p_x,\\sigma,e)$ ($\\sigma$ is the spin). These\n628\tindicate the fraction of each mode that is ``transmitted\" from\n629\tits high frequency form near the horizon out to infinity, while\n630\tthe rest is scattered back across the horizon. These coefficients\n631\thave not yet been calculated.\n632\t\n633\t\\section{ Quantum mechanics\n634\tof quasiparticles near the horizon.}\n635\t\n636\t\n637\tThe temperature and chemical potential of the Hawking radiation\n638\twere inferred above by exploiting the analogy with Hawking's calculation.\n639\tIt may be helpful here to exhibit the essential physics\n640\tin a simple way\\cite{DamourRuffini}.\n641\tNeglecting the spin degrees of freedom, the wave equation\n642\tfor the fermions is the same as in the bosonic case, which\n643\t(neglecting the electromagnetic field) is governed\n644\tby  the wave equation (1.1).\n645\tThe outgoing waves oscillate rapidly near the horizon. If we choose\n646\teigenmodes\n647\t$$\\Psi =\\Psi_{E,p_x}(z) e^{-iEt}e^{ ip_x x}e^{ip_y y}~~,\\eqno(7.1)$$\n648\tand neglect all terms without at least one $z$-derivative, eqn. (1.1)\n649\tbecomes\n650\t$$  [2i(-vE + p_x g^{xz}(z_h))\\partial_z+\\partial_z(g^{zz}(z)\n651\t\\partial_z )]\\Psi_{E,p_x}=0~~. \\eqno(7.2)$$\n652\tThe general outgoing  solution is:\n653\t$$\\Psi_{\\tilde E}(z) = a \\exp\\Bigl(2iv\\tilde E\\int^z dz'/ g^{zz}(z')\\Bigr)\n654\t$$\n655\t$$\\simeq a  \\exp\\Bigl(i(\\tilde E/\\kappa)\\ln(z-z_h)\\Bigr)~,\\eqno(7.3) $$\n656\twith $\\tilde E=E-p_xg^{xz}/v=E-p_x w$, where $w$ is the translational velocity\n657\tof the horizon (5.4) and $\\kappa$ is the surface gravity (5.6).\n658\t\n659\tThe outgoing modes that have purely negative frequency with respect to\n660\tthe free-fall frame (i.e. the superfluid frame) are states below the\n661\tFermi sea, which is in (or near) the\n662\tquantum ground state, as discussed above.\n663\tSome of these modes have {\\em positive} energy in the (stationary) soliton\n664\tframe however, so they may tunnel out away from the soliton.\n665\tThese modes fall into two classes according to whether $\\tilde E$ is\n666\tless than or greater than zero.  When $\\tilde E<0$, the positive energy\n667\tstates below\n668\tthe Fermi sea can be located {\\em outside} the horizon. Tunneling of these\n669\tstates is identified as due to level crossing in the ergoregion, and includes\n670\tthe Schwinger pairs when an electric field is included. When $\\tilde E>0$,\n671\tthe positive energy states below the Fermi sea can only exist {\\em behind}\n672\tthe horizon,\n673\tso it might seem that they could never tunnel out. However, this is not\n674\ttrue because these states always have an exponential tail that spills\n675\tout across the horizon. That they must have such a tail follows from the\n676\tfact that a purely negative frequency wavepacket must be analytic in the\n677\tupper half complex time plane. Equivalently, the mode function\n678\t$\\Psi_{\\tilde E}(z)$ must be analytic in the lower half complex $z$ plane.\n679\tAnalytic continuation of (7.3) across the horizon\n680\tin the lower half complex $z$ plane yields\n681\t$$\\theta(-u)\\, \\Psi_{\\tilde E}(z_h-u)+\n682\te^{-\\pi\\tilde E/\\kappa}\\, \\theta(u)\\, \\Psi_{\\tilde E}(z_h+u)~,\\eqno(7.4)$$\n683\twhere $u=z-z_h$.\n684\tThe second term is the tail term. The associated probability current\n685\tis the ratio of the squared norm of this piece to the total squared\n686\tnorm, i.e., it is $(e^{2\\pi\\tilde E/\\kappa}\\pm 1)^{-1}$, where\n687\t$\\pm=+$ for fermions and $-$ for bosons. (For bosons, the term\n688\tinside the horizon has negative norm in the relevant inner product.)\n689\tThe distribution of particles that tunnel across the horizon (in this\n690\tsense) is thus a thermal one at the Hawking temperature (restoring $\\hbar$)\n691\t$T_H=\\hbar\\kappa/2\\pi k_B$\n692\tand with the chemical potential\n693\t$p_x w$, in agreement with eqns. (6.1) and (6.3).\n694\tAfter tunneling across the horizon (so to speak), the particles are\n695\tpartially scattered back across the horizon. The fraction that\n696\tpropagate out to the asymptotic region is the emission coefficient\n697\t$\\Gamma$ of eqn. (6.2).\n698\t\n699\t\n700\t\\section{ Discussion.}\n701\t\n702\t\n703\tWith this moving texture model it should now be possible to study\n704\tsome of the questions presented by black hole horizons. The\n705\tHawking radiation, pair production in the ergoregion, and Schwinger\n706\tpair production are driven by the kinetic energy of the moving soliton,\n707\tand the back reaction will\n708\tbe to slow the soliton. The Hawking temperature is fairly constant\n709\tuntil, as $v$  approaches $c_\\perp$, $T_H$ goes to zero. This is\n710\tunlike the evaporation of a neutral black hole which gets hotter\n711\tas it shrinks. It is rather like the Hawking radiation from a\n712\tblack hole with a large magnetic charge which cannot be discharged\n713\tand so cools as it evaporates and approaches an extremal black hole.\n714\t\n715\tThe radiation from level crossing in the ergoregion\n716\tmay be observable with current technology, and\n717\tthe Hawking flux at $\\sim$ 5 $\\mu$K is probably not too low to be\n718\tobserved eventually.\n719\tThe Hawking temperature can be significantly\n720\thigher if instead of the soliton one takes a moving planar\n721\tinterface between $^3$He-A and $^3$He-B. The A-B interface has many\n722\tadvantages:\n723\tit can be moved with high velocity especially at low $T$\n724\t\\cite{Boyd} and the thickness $d$ of the interface is much shorter $d\\sim\n725\t500 \\AA$. This essentially increases the corresponding ``surface gravity\"\n726\tand the\n727\tHawking temperature.  But the ``nonrelativistic\" corrections\n728\talso become more important and this requires further investigations.\n729\tOn the other hand, for understanding some of the principal issues related to\n730\tevent horizons, it is not necessary to consider a real system. Gedanken\n731\texperiments can be made on model $^3$He-A-like systems, in which the\n732\t``nonrelativistic\" corrections can be made arbitrarily small.\n733\t\n734\tHorizons can occur in other moving\n735\ttopological and nontopological textures in\n736\tsuperfluids and superconductors, and for the bosonic degrees of freedom as well\n737\tas for the fermions. In particular, the orbital\n738\twaves in $^3$He-A  --- oscillations of the $\\hat l$ vector --- are\n739\tanalogous to\n740\telectromagnetic waves. At low $T$ their dynamics becomes\n741\trelativistic \\cite{Exotic} and one can discuss the propagation of such\n742\trelativistic bosons in textures with event horizons.\n743\t\n744\tAs for other topological objects, an interesting analogy\n745\toccurs in the case of quantized vortices, which correspond at\n746\tlarge distances to spinning cosmic strings\\cite{Volovik1997}.\n747\tThe vortex has fermion zero modes bound to the vortex core.\n748\tThere is a connection between the statistics of these fermion zero modes  and\n749\tthe fermionic zero modes on fundamental strings, which simulate the\n750\tthermodynamics of extreme black holes\n751\t\\cite{KopninVolovik1998}.  The Hawking radiation is absent if the vortex is\n752\tstationary with respect to the heat bath: a stationary\n753\tvortex corresponds to a local minimum of the energy and thus no radiation is\n754\tpossible from this state. If a\n755\tvortex moves with respect to the heat bath or if a nonaxisymmetric vortex core\n756\trotates with respect to the heat bath, the spectral flow\n757\tof the fermion zero modes lead to dissipation of the vortex\n758\tmotion and to an additional transverse force on the moving vortex\n759\t\\cite{KopninVolovik,Stone,KopninVolovik1997}. In some cases this corresponds to\n760\tthe appearance of a horizon with nonzero surface gravity\n761\t\\cite{KopninVolovik1998,KopninVolovik1997}.\n762\t\n763\tAnother interesting texture is a domain wall in a thin film of $^3$He-A,\n764\twhere the $\\hat l$-vector which is perpendicular to the film\n765\tchanges sign\\cite{SalomaaVolovik1989}.\n766\tIf this texture is moving the fermion quasiparticles see an effective\n767\t2+1 dimensional spacetime with black hole and white hole horizons\n768\tand a curvature singularity in between\\cite{JacobsonVolovik}. This is in many\n769\tways a much simpler system than the one discussed in this paper, since\n770\tthere is no ergoregion or (pseudo-)electromagnetic field.\n771\t\n772\tTo have a horizon\n773\tin a condensed matter system, it is not necessary to create curvature\n774\tsingularities as inside black holes, since the metric describing the horizon\n775\tdoes not follow from the Einstein equations. Moreover, if curvature\n776\tsingularities do occur, as in the thin film domain wall texture just mentioned,\n777\tthe physics is still under control.\n778\tThe quantum fermions propagating in\n779\tthe texture obey relativistic dynamics in the low-energy limit and thus\n780\tfully exhibit the quantum physics of the horizon, including both the\n781\tHawking radiation and the entropy of the fermion zero modes.\n782\tFor high enough energies, or inevitably near singularities in the\n783\ttexture, the fundamental nonrelativistic description takes over.\n784\tThus superfluid\n785\t$^3$He is a promising model for experimental and theoretical simulations of\n786\tquantum effects related to the event horizon, and may offer useful ideas\n787\tabout resolving the physics near a singularity.\n788\t\n789\t\n790\t\n791\t\\section{ Acknowledgements.}\n792\t\n793\tThis collaboration was carried out under the EU Human\n794\tCapital and Mobility Programme (contract CHGE-CT94-0069).
