Balbinot\\footnote{E-mail: balbinot@bo.infn.it}, S. Fagnocchi\n58\t\\footnote{E-mail: fagnocchi@bo.infn.it}\\\\\n59\t\\vspace*{0.2cm}\n60\t{\\it Dipartimento di Fisica dell' Universit\\`a di Bologna}\\\\\n61\t{\\it and INFN sezione di Bologna}\\\\\n62\t{\\it Via Irnerio 46, 40126 Bologna, Italy  }\\\\\n63\t\\vspace*{0.5cm}\n64\tand A. Fabbri\\footnote{E-mail: fabbria@bo.infn.it}\\\\\n65\t\\vspace*{0.2cm}\n66\t{\\it Departamento de Fisica Teorica, Facultad de Fisica, }\\\\\n67\t{\\it Universidad de Valencia, 46100-Burjassot, Valencia, Spain }\\\\\n68\t\\vspace*{3cm}\n69\t{ \\bf Abstract}\n70\t\\end{center}\n71\tWe investigate the backreaction equations for an acoustic black hole formed in a Laval\n72\tnozzle under the assumption that the motion of the fluid is one-dimensional. \n73\tThe solution in the near-horizon region shows that as phonons are (thermally) radiated \n74\tthe sonic horizon shrinks and the temperature decreases. This contrasts with the behaviour\n75\tof Schwarzschild black holes, and is similar to what happens in the evaporation of \n76\t(near-extremal) Reissner-Nordstr\\\"om black holes (i.e., infinite evaporation time). Finally, \n77\tby appropriate boundary conditions the solution is extended in both the asymptotic \n78\tregions of the nozzle.  \n79\t\n80\t\n81\t\n82\t\\bigskip\n83\t%\\bigskip\n84\t\\noindent PACS: 04.62.+v, 04.70.Dy, 47.40.Ki.\n85\t\\\\Keywords: Acoustic black holes, Hypersonic flow, Hawking radiation, Backreaction. \n86\t\\vfill\n87\t\\setcounter{page}{0}\n88\t\\setcounter{footnote}{0}\n89\t\\newpage\n90\t\n91\t\\section{Introduction}\n92\t\n93\tIn 1974 Hawking \\cite{hawking} announced to the physical community his famous result: \n94\tblack holes are not black at all, but emit thermal radiation at a temperature \n95\tproportional to the horizon surface gravity. \n96\tHawking came to this remarkable conclusion by examining, within the framework of quantum \n97\tfield theory in curved space, the propagation of a massless scalar field in the geometry \n98\tof a collapsing body forming a black hole. If one assumes spherical symmetry, \n99\tthe space-time in the region exterior to the body is described by the Schwarzschild solution \n100\t(Birkhoff theorem). \n101\tFor these kinds of black holes the horizon is located at $r=2M$ \n102\t($M$ is the black hole mass) and its surface gravity is $k=1/4M$. This yields an emission \n103\ttemperature $T_H=\\frac{\\hbar k}{2\\pi}=\\frac{\\hbar}{8\\pi M}$\n104\t(the velocity of light and Boltzman constant are set to one). \n105\tAs a consequence black holes, \n106\tthe final end-state of gravitational collapse according to classical General Relativity, \n107\tare unstable. \n108\t\\\\The actual evolution of an evaporating black hole should in priciple be \n109\tdescribed (until quantum gravity effects become relevant) by the semiclassical Einstein equations (backreaction equations)\n110\t\\be \n111\t\\label{Gback}\n112\tG_{\\mu\\nu}(g_{\\alpha\\beta})=8\\pi \\langle T_{\\mu\\nu}(g_{\\alpha\\beta})\\rangle\\ ,\n113\t\\ee\n114\twhere $G_{\\mu\\nu}$ is the Einstein tensor and the r.h.s. is the expectation value \n115\tof the quantum stress tensor for the matter fields which drive the evaporation.\n116\t\\\\ Eq. (\\ref {Gback}) has to be solved for the evaporating black hole metric \n117\t$g_{\\alpha\\beta}$. This requires the knowledge of $\\langle T_{\\mu\\nu}(g_{\\alpha\\beta})\\rangle$\n118\t for an arbitrary (let's say spherically symmetric) metric.\n119\tUnfortunately, because of the extreme difficulty of the problem, no such expression is \n120\tavailable and the backreaction is usually modelled by extrapolating Hawkings's result, \n121\twhich is strictly valid only for static or stationary black holes. \n122\tTherefore a spherically symmetric black hole of mass $M(t)$ is supposed to emit radiation at a temperature $T=\\hbar (8\\pi\n123\tM(t))^{-1}$. Because of this emission, it looses mass at a rate given by the Stefan-Boltzman law $\\frac{dM}{dt}\\simeq\n124\t-AT^4\\simeq -1/M^2$, where $A=16 \\pi M^2$ is the horizon area.\n125\tAs the mass decreases the black hole becomes hotter, as can be seen from the temperature \n126\tformula given above, and eventually disappears (with a final explosion?). Its lifetime is of the order $M_0^3$ where $M_0$ is the initial mass of the black hole. \n127\t\\\\If the black hole possesses a conserved electric charge $Q$ ($|Q|<M$) the picture is quite different. In this case the space-time is described by the Reissner-Nordstr\\\"om solution for which the surface gravity reads\n128\t\\be\n129\t\\kappa=(r_+ -M)/r_+^2\n130\t\\ee\n131\twhere $r_+$ is the radius of the horizon, i.e.  $r_+=M+\\sqrt{M^2-Q^2}$.\n132\tOne sees that, for near-extremal black holes ($M\\stackrel{\\sim}{>}|Q|$), as the mass of the hole decreases because of the evaporation, the temperature $T=\\frac{\\hbar}{2\\pi}k$ drops costantly.\n133\tWhen $M$ is reduced to $M=|Q|$ the temperature is zero.\n134\tThis final state (remnant) is reached in infinite time. This corresponds to the so called third law of black hole thermodynamics.\n135\t\n136\tIn 1981 a remarkable paper of Unruh \\cite{unruh81} appeared showing that a quantum emission similar to the \n137\tone predicted by Hawking for black holes is expected in a seemingly completely different physical context, namely fluids\n138\tundergoing hypersonic motion. This far reaching result opened a continuously developing field of research (the so called\n139\tblack hole analogue models \\cite{libro}) in condensed matter physics where, unike gravity, the hope to perform experimental test on these theoretical predictions does not seem so remote.\n140\t\\\\In this paper we will give a first  insight on   the backreaction this  emitted radiation has on the fluid.\n141\tThe plan of the paper is the following.\n142\t\\\\In section II we report Unruh's analysis of the sound  propagating  in a hypersonic fluid within the action formalism which is then used to write the backreaction equations for the fluid motion.\n143\t\\\\In section III we introduce a lower dimensional model where the backreaction equations can be solved to find the first order in $\\hbar$ correction to the classical flow.\n144\t\\\\In section IV we evaluate the quantum stress tensor for the classical background to be inserted in the backreaction equations.\n145\t\\\\In section V we solve the backreaction equations near the sonic horizon.\n146\t\\\\In section VI and VII the near horizon solution is extended in the asymptotic regions \n147\tthrough the imposition of appropriate matching conditions.\n148\t\\\\Section VIII is devoted to the conclusions and some extrapolations of our results.\n149\t\\\\In Appendix A and B we report tecnical details needed to perform the calculations.\n150\t\n151\t\n152\t\n153\t%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%\n154\t\n155\t\\sect{Hypersonic flow and sonic black holes}\n156\t\n157\tUnruh considered an irrotational, homentropic fluid. In this case the Eulerian equations of motion can be derived from the action\n158\t\\be\n159\t\\label {Sclassic}\n160\tS=-\\int d^4 x \\left[ \\r \\dot{\\f}+\\half \\r (\\nabla \\f)^2+u(\\r)\\right]\n161\t\\ee\n162\twhere $\\r$ is the mass density, $\\f$ the velocity potential, i.e. $\\overrightarrow{v}=\\overrightarrow{\\nabla}\\f$, and $u$ the internal energy density. The overdot means differentiation with respect to (newtonian) time.\n163\t\n164\tVarying $S$ with respect to $\\f$ yields the continuity equation\n165\t\\be\n166\t\\label{Eqcont}\n167\t\\dot {\\r}+\\overrightarrow{\\nabla}\\cdot (\\r \\overrightarrow{v})=0\\ ,\n168\t\\ee\n169\twhereas variation with respect to $\\r$ gives Bernoulli's equation\n170\t\\be\n171\t\\label {Ber}\n172\t\\dot{\\f}+\\half\\overrightarrow{v}^2+\\mu(\\r)=0\\ ,\n173\t\\ee\n174\twhere $\\mu(\\r)=\\frac{du}{d\\r}$.\n175\t\n176\tOne can now obtain the linearized wave equation for the propagation of sound waves in a background mean flow by replacing\n177\t\\bea\n178\t\\f&\\rightarrow&\\f+\\f_1\\ ,\\\\\n179\t\\r&\\rightarrow&\\r+\\r_1 \\ ,\\nonumber\n180\t\\eea\n181\twhere $\\r$ and $\\f$ define the mean flow; they are assumed to satisfy the equations of motion and $\\f_1$ and $\\r_1$ are small amplitudes perturbations.\n182\t\\\\ Expanding $S$ up to quadratic order in these perturbations one obtains\n183\t\\bea\n184\t\\label{S}\n185\tS&=&S_0-\\int d^4 x \\left[ \\r_1 \\dot{\\f}_1+\\half \\frac{c^2}{\\r} \\r_1^2+\\half \\r (\\overrightarrow{\\nabla} \\f_1)^2+\\r_1\\overrightarrow{v} \\cdot  \\overrightarrow{\\nabla} \\f_1 \\right]\\\\\n186\t&=&S_0+S_2\\ .\\nonumber\n187\t\\eea\n188\tThe speed of sound $c$ is defined as \n189\t\\be\n190\t\\label{defc}\n191\tc^2= \\r \\frac{d\\mu}{d\\r} \\ . \\ee\n192\t\n193\tOne can derive the equation of motion for $\\r_1$\n194\t\\be\n195\t\\label{romotion}\n196\t\\r_1=-\\frac{\\r}{c^2}\\left( \\dot{\\f}_1+\\overrightarrow{v} \\cdot  \n197\t\\overrightarrow{\\nabla} \\f_1\\right) \\ .\n198\t\\ee\n199\tSince $\\r_1$    occurs    quadratically in (\\ref{S}) we may use eq. (\\ref{romotion}) \n200\tto eliminate it and obtain an action for the potential $\\f_1$ only\n201\t\\be\n202\t\\label{s}\n203\tS_2=-\\int d^4 x \\left[ \\half \\r (\\overrightarrow{\\nabla} \\f_1)^2\n204\t-\\frac{\\r}{2c^2} ( \\dot{\\f}_1 +\\overrightarrow{v} \\cdot  \\overrightarrow{\\nabla} \\f_1 )^2 \n205\t\\right] \\ .\n206\t\\ee\n207\tThe remarkable thing is that $S_2$ can be written as \n208\t\\be\n209\t\\label{sgr}\n210\tS_2=-\\half \\int d^4 x \\dt g^{\\mu\\nu} \\p_\\mu \\f_1 \\p_\\nu \\f_1 \\ ,\n211\t\\ee\n212\twhere, following Unruh, we have introduced the acoustic metric\n213\t\\be \\label{acmio}\n214\tg_{\\mu\\nu}=-\\frac{\\r}{c}\\left(\n215\t\\begin{array}{cc}\n216\tc^2-v^2&\\overrightarrow{v}^T\\\\\n217\t\\overrightarrow{v}&-I\n218\t\\end{array}\n219\t\\right)\n220\t\\ee\n221\tand $I$ is the three-dimensional identity matrix.\\\\ \n222\tIn the form of eq. (\\ref{sgr}) $S_2$ is completely equivalent to the action for a \n223\tmassless scalar field $\\f_1$ propagating in a curved space-time whose line element is\n224\t\\be\n225\tds^2=g_{\\mu\\nu} dx^\\mu dx^\\nu \\ .\n226\t\\ee\n227\tVarying the action (\\ref{sgr}) with respect to $\\f_1$ gives the sound wave equation which can be written in a simple and elegant geometrical way\n228\t$$\n229\t\\Box \\f_1=0 \\ , \n230\t$$ \n231\twhere $\\Box=\\nabla_\\mu \\nabla^\\mu$ is the covariant derivative with respect to the acoustic \n232\tmetric $g_{\\mu\\nu}$.\n233\tVariation of $S_2$ of eq. (\\ref{sgr}) with respect to the acoustic metric gives the so called \n234\t``pseudo energy momentum tensor'' (PEMT) $T_{\\mu\\nu}$ \n235\t\\be\n236\tT_{\\mu\\nu}=-\\frac{2}{\\sqrt{-g}}\\frac{\\delta S_2}{\\delta g^{\\mu\\nu}}\\ .\\ee\n237\tAs discussed by Stone \\cite{stone} the invariance of $S_2$ under diffeomorphisms implies\n238\tthe covariant conservation of $T_{\\mu\\nu}$ \n239\t\\be\n240\tT^{\\mu\\ ;\\nu}_{\\ \\nu}=0 \\ , \n241\t\\ee\n242\twhich describes in a nice compact form the exchange of energy and momentum between the waves\n243\tand the fluid reproducing various known laws of classical fluid motion. Of particular interest\n244\tare fluids undergoing hypersonic motion.  \n245\tIn this case the region of the fluid for which $\\overrightarrow{v}^2 > c^2$ is called acoustic black  hole,\n246\tits boundary $ \\overrightarrow{v}^2=c^2$  defines the sonic horizon. \n247\tFrom this region sound waves cannot propagate upstream since the fluid velocity is bigger \n248\tthan the sound velocity. Sound is dragged by the fluid and cannot excape.\n249\t\\\\Using the same arguments of Hawking, Unruh, quantizing the field $\\f_1$,\n250\tshowed that in the formation of a sonic hole one expects a thermal emission \n251\tof phonons at a temperature\n252\t\\be\n253\tT=\\frac{\\hbar  k}{2\\pi  c}\\ ,\n254\t\\ee\n255\twhere $k$ is the surface gravity of the sonic horizon \\cite{visser}\n256\t\\be\n257\tk=\\left. \\half \\frac{d}{dn}(c^2-|\\overrightarrow{v}_\\bot |^2)\\right|_H \\ ,\n258\t\\ee\n259\t$n$ is the normal to the horizon.\n260\t\n261\tA tipical situation where this is supposed to occur is a Laval nozzle \n262\tdepicted in Fig.1.\n263\t%\\begin{figure}\n264\t%\\centerline{\\psfig{figure=laval.ps,width=2.6in,height=1.7in,angle=-90}}\n265\t%\\end{figure}\n266\t%\\begin{center}\n267\t%\\makebox[8.5cm]{\\parbox{8.5cm} {\\small FIG.1: A Laval nozzle. On the right of the waist (the sonic horizon) the fluid is\n268\t%subsonic, while on the left it is hypersonic (the sonic black hole). }}\n269\t%\\end{center}\n270\t\\begin{figure}\n271\t%\\includegraphics[angle=270,width=3.4in,clip]{laval.ps}\n272\t\\centerline{\\psfig{figure=laval.ps,width=2.6in,height=1.7in,angle=-90}}\n273\t\\caption{A Laval nozzle. The waist of the\n274\tnozzle represents the sonic horizon ($|\\vec v|=c$). In the region on the right of the waist $|\\vec v|<c$\n275\tand on the left $|\\vec v|>c$ (sonic hole).}\n276\t\\label{fig1}\n277\t\\end{figure}  \n278\tThe fluid flows from right to left; at the waist of the nozzle the fluid velocity reaches the speed of sound. This is the location of the sonic horizon. \n279\t\\\\Expanding into the left region the velocity increases and the fluid becomes hypersonic; this region describes the acoustic black  hole. In the asymptotic right region a thermal radiation of phonons is expected according to Unruh's analysis.\n280\t\\\\The aim of this paper is to give a first qualitative description of the effects this emitted radiation has on the fluid dynamics, i.e. the backreaction for acoustic black holes.\n281\t\\\\To this end we have to establish the analogue of the semiclassical Einstein equations (\\ref{Gback}), i.e. the evolution equation for the fluid driven by the quantum fields.\n282\t%One can take into account first order (in $\\hbar$) quantum corrections to the classical\n283\t%motion of the fluid by writing the relevant action as $\\Gamma=S+ S_q$, where $S$ is the classical action (\\ref{Sclassic}) and $S_q$ is the effective action for the quantum fields. From the previous discussion one sees that  $S_q$ is a functional of the acoustic metric, which \n284\t\\\\Using standard background field formalism one writes the fundamental quantum \n285\tfields as a sum of background fields ($\\rho, \\psi$) (not necessarily satisfying the\n286\tclassical equations of motion) plus quantum fluctuations. Integrating out the quantum\n287\tfluctuations one obtains the one-loop effective action formally defined as\n288\t\\be\n289\t\\Gamma=S + \\frac{1}{2}\\hbar Tr\\ln\\left[\\Box_{g(\\rho,\\vec v)}\\right] + O(\\hbar^2)\\ ,\n290\t\\ee\n291\twhere $S$ is the classical action (\\ref{Sclassic}) and $\\Box_{g(\\rho,\\vec v)}$ is the\n292\tD�Alembertian calculated from an acoustic metric $g_{\\mu\\nu}(\\rho, \\vec v)$ of the functional \n293\tform of eq. (\\ref{acmio}) \\cite{bavili}. We assume the divergences in the determinant of the\n294\tabove effective action to be removed by employing a covariant regularization scheme. \n295\tThis is the key hypothesis of our work. We will comment on it in the conclusion section. \n296\tOne can therefore write $\\Gamma=S+S_q(g_{\\mu\\nu}(\\rho,\\vec v))$, where the quantum part of\n297\t$\\Gamma$ depends on the dynamical variables $\\rho, \\vec v$ only through the acoustic metric \n298\t(this is a direct consequence of our hypothesis) and  \n299\tcoincides with the effective action of a massless scalar field propagating \n300\tin a curved background whose metric is $g_{\\mu\\nu}(\\rho, \\vec v)$. \n301\t% We can formally write\n302\t%\\be\n303\t%e^{-S_q(g_{\\alpha\\beta})}=\\int D\\f_1 e^{-S_2(g_{\\alpha\\beta},\\f_1)/\\hbar}\\ .\n304\t%\\ee\n305\t\\\\Given this it follows that, using the chain rule,\n306\t\\bea\n307\t\\frac{\\d S_q}{\\d \\r}&=&\\frac{\\d S_q}{\\d g^{\\mu\\nu}}\\frac{\\d g^{\\mu\\nu}}{\\d \\r}\n308\t=-\\frac{\\sqrt{-g}}{2} \\langle T_{\\mu\\nu}\\rangle \\frac{\\d g^{\\mu\\nu}}{\\d \\r}\n309\t=\\frac{\\sqrt{-g}}{2} \\langle T_{\\mu\\nu}\\rangle \\left( \\frac{1}{\\r}\\right)g^{\\mu\\nu}\\\\\n310\t&=&\\half \\frac{\\sqrt{-g}}{\\r} \\langle T\\rangle =\\half \\langle T\\rangle \\frac{\\r}{c}\\ ,\\nonumber\n311\t\\eea\n312\twhere \n313\t\\be\n314\t\\langle T_{\\mu\\nu}\\rangle \\equiv -\\frac{2}{\\sqrt{-g}}\\frac{\\d S_q}{\\d g^{\\mu\\nu}}\n315\t\\ee\n316\tand $\\langle T\\rangle =\\langle T^\\mu_\\mu\\rangle $.\\\\\n317\tSimilarly\n318\t\\bea\n319\t\\frac{\\d S_q}{\\d v_i}&=&\\frac{\\d S_q}{\\d g^{\\mu\\nu}}\\frac{\\d g^{\\mu\\nu}}{\\d v_i}\n320\t=-\\frac{\\sqrt{-g}}{2} \\langle T_{\\mu\\nu}\\rangle \\frac{\\d g^{\\mu\\nu}}{\\d v_i}=\\\\\n321\t&=&\\frac{\\r}{c}(\\langle T_{ti}\\rangle +v_i \\langle T_{ii}\\rangle ) \\ .\\nonumber\n322\t\\eea\n323\tIn the above expression $g^{\\mu\\nu}$ is the inverse metric, i.e. \n324\t\\be\n325\tg^{\\mu\\nu}=-\\frac{1}{\\r c}\\left(\n326\t\\begin{array}{cc}\n327\t1&\\overrightarrow{v}^T\\\\\n328\t\\overrightarrow{v}& \\overrightarrow{v}\\overrightarrow{v}^T-c^2 I\n329\t\\end{array}\n330\t\\right)\\ .\n331\t\\ee\n332\t% where $\\r$ and $v$ are now arbitrary space-time functions that do not necessarily satisfy the classical equations of motion. \n333\t\\\\The backreaction equations are  therefore (taking into account that $g_{\\mu\\nu}$ does not \n334\tdepend on $\\dot{\\f}$)\n335\t\\bea\n336\t\\label{eqbackA}\n337\t&\\dot {\\r}+\\overrightarrow{\\nabla}\\cdot \n338\t(\\r \\overrightarrow{v})-\\nabla_i \\left( \\frac{\\r}{c}(\\langle T_{ti}\\rangle +v_i \n339\t\\langle T_{ii}\\rangle ) \\right)=0&\\ ,\\\\\n340\t\\label{eqbackB}\n341\t&\\dot{\\f}+\\half\\overrightarrow{v}^2+\\mu(\\r)-  \\half \\frac{\\r}{c}\\langle T\\rangle =0\\ .&\n342\t\\eea\n343\tThe $\\langle T_{\\mu\\nu}\\rangle $ appearing in the backreaction equations \n344\tshould be considered as expectation value of the quantum pseudo \n345\tenergy momentum \n346\ttensor operator taken in a quantum state appropriate for  the radiation process, namely the analogue of the Unruh state\n347\t\\cite{unruh76} (the quantum state suitable to describe black hole evaporation at late times),\n348\tin which in the remote past prior to the formation of the sonic hole the quantum field is\n349\tin its vacuum state. \n350\t\\\\Inspection of the backreaction equations reveals that the continuity equation \n351\t(associated to the symmetry $\\psi\\to \\psi + const.$ of the effective action) \n352\tgets modified \n353\tby including the divergence of\n354\tthe phonons momentum density ($\\sqrt{-g}\\langle T^0_i\\rangle$),\n355\t%quantum flux (note that $\\langle T_{ti}\\rangle +v_i \\langle T_{ii}\\rangle \n356\t%\\propto \\langle T^t_i\\rangle )$, \n357\twhereas the Bernoulli equation gets an additional contribution to the chemical potential\n358\tgiven by a term\n359\tproportional to the trace of the pseudo energy momentum tensor of the phonons.\n360\tThese equations reflect the underlying two-component structure of the system as in the\n361\tLandau-Khalatnikov theory of superfluidity \\cite{khalatnikov}.\\\n362\t\\\\As in the black hole case the general expression of $S_q$ and \n363\t$\\langle T_{\\mu\\nu}(g_{\\alpha\\beta})\\rangle $ \n364\tis completely unknown and no explicit solution of the backreaction equations (\\ref{eqbackA}), \n365\t(\\ref{eqbackB}) can be given. \n366\t  \n367\t%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%\n368\t\\sect{The dimensional reduction model}\n369\t\n370\tLower dimensional models are very useful in physics as they allow explicit solutions of the \n371\tdynamical equations to be found, providing at least  a qualitative description of the \n372\tevolution of real four-dimensional systems. \n373\tThis attitude has been largely used in studying quantum effects in black hole physics, \n374\twhere two-dimensional models enable  investigation of the so called \"s-wave sector\" \n375\t\\cite{strominger}. The most popular one is the one proposed by Callan-Giddings-Harvey-Strominger\n376\t(CGHS) \\cite{cghs} in which the 4D quantum stress tensor is replaced by a 2D one associated to a\n377\tminimally coupled massless scalar field described at the quantum level by the Polyakov action.\n378\tThis approximation neglects backscattering of the quantum fields caused by the potential barrier\n379\tlocated near the horizon. \\\\\n380\tWithin this philosophy a qualitative insight in the backreaction going on in a hypersonic\n381\tfluid can be obtained by assuming a one dimensional flow for the fluid; the relevant\n382\tphysical quantities depend only on the $z$ coordinate running along the axis of the Laval\n383\tnozzle of Fig. 1 (i.e. velocity components along $x$ and $y$ are negligible with respect to the\n384\t$z$ component). \n385\t\\\\The effective action for the CGHS-like model for the fluid quantum dynamics can be given as\n386\t$\\Gamma^{(2)}=S^{(2)}+S_{pol}$, where \n387\t% \\\\After integrating over the transverse coordinates $x$, $y$, the classical action (\\ref{Sclassic}) can therefore be written\n388\t\\be \n389\tS^{(2)}=-\\int d^2 x A  \\left[ \\r \\dot{\\f}+\\half \\r (\\p_z \\f)^2+u(\\r)\\right]  \n390\t\\ee\n391\tis obtained integrating $S$ over the transverse coordinates $x, y$ and \n392\t$A$ is the area of the transverse section of the nozzle. \n393\t%The classical equations of motion following from $S^{(2)}$ are\n394\t%\\bea\n395\t%\\frac{\\d S^{(2)}}{\\d \\f}=0 &\\Longrightarrow& \\p_t(A\\r)+\\p_z(A\\r v)=0\\ ,\\\\\n396\t%\\frac{\\d S^{(2)}}{\\d \\r}=0 &\\Longrightarrow& A(\\dot{\\f}+\\half v^2+\\mu(\\r))=0\\ ,\n397\t%\\eea\n398\t%where $v=\\p_z \\f$.\n399\t%\\\\Since $A$ is time independent one has\n400\t%\\bea\n401\t%\\label{C2}\n402\t%&A\\dot{\\r}+\\p_z(A\\r v)=0\\ ,& \\\\\n403\t%\\label{B2}\n404\t%&\\dot{\\f}+\\half v^2+\\mu(\\r)=0\\ . &\n405\t%\\eea\n406\t%The action for the quadratic fluctuations (\\ref{s}) can be written as\n407\t%\\be\n408\t%S_2^{(2)}=\\int d^2 x A \\frac{\\r}{c}\\sqrt{-g^{(2)}} g^{(2)ab}\\half \\p_a\\f_1\\p_b\\f_1 \\ , \n409\t%\\ee\n410\t%where\n411\t%\\be\n412\t%\\label{metric2}\n413\t%g_{ab}^{(2)}=-\\frac{\\r}{c}\\left(\n414\t%\\begin{array}{cc}\n415\t%c^2-v^2&v\\\\\n416\t%v&-1\n417\t%\\end{array}\n418\t%\\right)\n419\t%\\ee \n420\t%$a,b={z,t}$; $g_{ab}^{(2)}$ \n421\t%is the $z,t$-section of the acoustic metric of eq. (\\ref{sgr}) under the assumption \n422\t%$v=v(z,t)$, $\\r=\\r(z,t)$. The action $S_2^{(2)}$ describes now a two-dimensional massless \n423\t%scalar field $\\f_1(z,t)$ propagating in the two-dimensional metric $g_{ab}^{(2)}(z,t)$ \n424\t%coupled not only to this metric but also to a ``dilaton\" field $e^{-2\\phi}=\\frac{A\\r}{c}$,  \n425\t%which is the proper area of the transverse section and is a remnant of the \n426\t%four-dimensional origin of $S_2^{(2)}$.\n427\t%\\\\Functional integration of the $\\f_1$ field yields $S_q^{(2)}(g_{ab}^{(2)},\\f)$, the effective action for the quantum fluctuations which is a functional of the 2D metric and the dilaton. \n428\t%\\\\The backreaction equations for the lower dimensional model can be obtained \n429\t%by the same procedure of section 2, starting from the action $\\Gamma^{(2)}=S^{(2)}+ S_q^{(2)}$.\n430\t%\\\\Introducing the 2D quantum pseudo energy momentum tensor as\n431\t%\\be\n432\t%\\langle T_{ab}^{(2)}\\rangle =\\frac{2}{\\sqrt{-g^{(2)}}}\\frac{\\d S^{(2)}}{\\d g^{(2)ab}}\n433\t%\\ee\n434\t%we have \n435\t%\\bea\n436\t%\\label{dSdrho}\n437\t%\\frac{\\d S^{(2)}_q}{\\d \\r}&=&-\\half \\frac{\\sqrt{-g^{(2)}}}{\\r}\\langle T^{(2)}\\rangle\n438\t%+\\frac{\\d S^{(2)}_q}{\\d \\phi}\\frac{\\d \\phi}{\\d \\r}=-\\half \\left(\\langle T^{(2)}\\rangle\n439\t%+\\langle P_T\\rangle \\right)\\ , \\\\\n440\t%\\label{dSdv}\n441\t%\\frac{\\d S^{(2)}_q}{\\d v}&=&-\\frac{1}{c}(\\langle T_{zt}\\rangle +v\\langle T_{zz}\\rangle )\\ , \n442\t%\\eea\n443\t%where $P_T$ is the transverse pressure.\\\\\n444\tUsing the chain rule as before one can write \n445\tthe backreaction equations as\n446\t\\bea\n447\t\\label{back1}\n448\t&&A\\dot{\\r}+\\p_z(A\\r v)+\\p_z \\left[ -\\frac{1}{c}(\\langle T^{(2)}_{tz}\\rangle \n449\t+v\\langle T^{(2)}_{zz}\\rangle )\\right]=0\n450\t\\ , \\\\\n451\t\\label{back2}\n452\t&&A\\left( \\dot{\\f}+\\frac{v^2}{2}+\\mu(\\r) \\right)\n453\t-\\frac{1}{2} \\left(\\langle T^{(2)}\\rangle  \\right)\n454\t=0\\ ,\n455\t\\eea\n456\twhere\n457\t\\be\n458\t\\langle T_{ab}^{(2)}\\rangle =-\\frac{2}{\\sqrt{-g^{(2)}}}\\frac{\\delta S_{pol}}{\\delta g^{(2)ab}}\n459\t\\ee\n460\tand $g_{ab}^{(2)}$ is the ($t,z$) section of the acoustic metric (\\ref{sgr})\n461\t\\be\n462\t\\label{metric2}\n463\tg_{ab}^{(2)}=-\\frac{\\r}{c}\\left(\n464\t\\begin{array}{cc}\n465\tc^2-v^2&v\\\\\n466\tv&-1\n467\t\\end{array}\n468\t\\right) \\ .\n469\t\\ee \n470\t \n471\t%The expectation values entering the backreaction equations (in 4D and in the reduced 2D model)\n472\t%are formally divergent and a meaning has to be given with an appropriate renormalization\n473\t%scheme which makes them finite. As we have stressed before, at the classical level various laws\n474\t%of fluid motion can be rewritten as covariant conservation of the PEMT, furthermore these\n475\t%conservation laws may all be interpreted in terms of semiclassical motion of phonons\n476\t%\\cite{stone}. Therefore we assume that the expectation values of the PEMT should be \n477\t%regularized using a covariant renormalization scheme. This is also the attitude followed by\n478\t%the authors of Ref. \\cite{bavili}. \n479\t%Coming back to our 2D model, we note that \n480\t%the action $S_2^{(2)} $ is Weyl invariant. \n481\t%Given our assumption on the regularization scheme to be used it follows that\n482\t% $T^{(2)}$ is completely anomalous and can be written in terms of\n483\t%local geometric quantities \\cite{grav} as \n484\t%\\be\n485\t%\\label{traccia}\n486\t%\\langle T^{(2)}\\rangle =\\frac{\\hbar}{24 \\pi}\\left[ R^{(2)}-6(\\nabla\\phi)^2+6\\Box\\phi\\right]\\ ,\n487\t%\\ee\n488\t%where $R^{(2)}$ is the Ricci scalar of the metric $g_{ab}^{(2)}$, \n489\t%$(\\nabla\\phi)^2=g^{ab (2)}\\p_a\\phi\\p_b \\phi$ and \n490\t%$\\Box=\\nabla_a\\nabla^a$, $\\nabla$ being the covariant derivative operator.\n491\t\n492\t%Even for this simplified model the effective action $S^{(2)}_q$ is not explicitly known. \n493\t%From the trace anomaly only a part of $S^{(2)}_q$ can be reconstructed: \n494\t%this is the so called ``anomaly induced effective action\". The Weyl invariant part is unknown \n495\t%(see \\cite{bafa} for a discussion of this problem). To make the computation feasible we will neglect \n496\t%the transverse pressure term in eq. (\\ref{dSdrho}) and approximate the quantum flux term \n497\t%in eq. (\\ref{back1}) by the corresponding Polyakov expression, \n498\t%as we will describe in the next section.\n499\t%\\\\Studies of gravitational black hole evaporation have shown that this approximation \n500\t%is quite reasonable near the horizon of\n501\t%the hole and asymptotically. Various models of 2D black holes like CGHS\n502\t%\\cite{CGHS} and RST \\cite{RST} are contructed in this way.\n503\tOur aim is to solve these backreaction equations to first order in $\\hbar$ to calculate \n504\tthe first quantum corrections to the classical fluid configuration. \n505\tTherefore we need the quantum source terms calculated at zero order in $\\hbar$, i.e. for the classical solution.\n506\t\n507\t\n508\t\n509\t%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%\n510\t\n511\t\\sect{The quantum pseudo stress tensor for static sonic black holes}\n512\t\n513\tBefore undertaking the study of the backreaction in  eqs. (\\ref{back1}), (\\ref{back2})  \n514\tlet us describe the solution of the classical equations of motion which describes a static \n515\tacoustic black  hole and then find the corresponding $\\langle T^{(2)}_{ab}\\rangle $ \n516\tin the Unruh state \n517\tfor this background. The classical equations of motion are given by eqs. (\\ref{back1}), \n518\t(\\ref{back2}) neglecting the phonon quantum contribution. \n519\t\\\\Assuming steady flow, i.e. no time dependence, the continuity equation (\\ref{back1}) yields\n520\t\\be\n521\t\\label{cont2}\n522\tA(z)\\r(z)v(z)=const \\equiv D \\ , \n523\t\\ee\n524\twhereas the Bernoulli equation simplifies to \n525\t\\be \\label{nbe}\n526\t\\frac{v^2}{2}+\\mu(\\rho)=0\\ .\\ee\n527\tDifferentiating both equations and taking into account the definition of the velocity of sound\n528\t(eq. (\\ref{defc})) one easily gets\n529\t\\be\n530\t\\frac{A'}{A}=-\\frac{v'}{v}(1-\\frac{v^2}{c^2})\\ ,\n531\t\\ee\n532\twhich is the famous nozzle equation. From this one deduces important features of the fluid\n533\tmotion. First of all the horizon ($|v|=c$) forms at the waist of the nozzle\n534\t($A'=0$).\\footnote{Note that this is in general not true if external forces are present.\n535\tIn that case, the equation giving the location of the sonic horizon is $A'/A=-f/\\r c^2$,\n536\twhere $f$ is the external force (see the second of Refs. \\cite{garayvisser}). }\n537\tFurthermore in the hypersonic region ($|v|>c$) the velocity increases together with the section\n538\tof the nozzle, just the opposite of what happens in the more familiare subsonic ($|v|<c$)\n539\tcase.\n540\t\\\\Let us further assume the sound velocity $c$ constant.\n541\t% so integration of eq. (\\ref{defc}) fixes $\\mu$ as a function of $\\r$, namely\n542\t%\\be\n543\t%\\mu=c^2 \\ln \\frac{\\r}{\\r_0}\n544\t%\\ee\n545\t%with constant $\\r_0$.\n546\tThis allows the Bernoulli equation (\\ref{nbe}) to be written as\n547\t\\be\n548\t\\half v^2+c^2\\ln \\frac{\\r}{\\r_0}=0\\ ,\n549\t\\ee\n550\ti.e.\n551\t\\be\n552\t\\label{rho}\n553\t\\r=\\r_0 e^{-\\frac{v^2}{2c^2}}\\ .\n554\t\\ee\n555\tLet us choose the profile of the Laval nozzle as \n556\t\\be\n557\t\\label{area}\n558\tA=\n559\t\\left\\{\n560\t\\begin {array}{rl}\n561\tA_0+\\beta z^2 & \\mbox {for}|z|\\leq z_0\\\\\n562\tA_+=const & \\mbox {for}|z|> z_0\n563\t\\end{array}\n564\t\\right.\n565\t\\ee\n566\twhere $A_0$, $\\beta$ and $z_0$ are constants.\n567\t\\\\From the continuity equation (\\ref{cont2}) one has for $|z|\\leq z_0$\n568\t\\be\n569\t\\label{z2}\n570\tz^2=\\frac{1}{\\beta}\\left[ \\frac{D}{\\r_0}\\frac{e^{v^2/2c^2}}{v} -A_0   \\right]\\ .\n571\t\\ee\n572\tThe sonic horizon is located at $z=0$ where $v=-c$ (remember that the fluid is moving \n573\tfrom right to left). The constant $D$ in eq. (\\ref{cont2}) can be evaluated as\n574\t\\be\n575\t-A_0\\r_0 e^{-\\half}c=D \\ ,\n576\t\\ee\n577\twhich when inserted in eq. (\\ref{z2}) yields\n578\t\\be\n579\tz^2=\\frac{A_0}{\\beta}\\left[ \\frac{c}{|v|}e^{\\frac{v^2-c^2}{2c^2}} -1   \\right]\\ .\n580\t\\ee\n581\tThis implicitly defines $v=v(z)$ and from eq. (\\ref{rho}) we have $\\r(z)$; \n582\tso for $|z|\\leq z_0$ the acoustic metric $g_{ab}^{(2)}(z)$ of the static sonic black hole \n583\tis determined. \\\\ \\noindent For $|z|>z_0$ the solution is simply $v(z)=\\mbox{const}=v(z_0)$\n584\tfor $z>z_0$ and $v(z)=\\mbox{const}=v(-z_0)$ for $z<-z_0$. Similarly for $\\r(z)$.\n585\tNote that $|v(z)|$ increases as $z$ decreases, while $\\r(z)$  decreases as $z$ decreases.\n586\tThis resulting acoustic metric should be regarded as the asymptotic configuration\n587\tof the fluid resulting from the (time dependent) formation of the sonic hole (see for\n588\texample \\cite{balisovi}).\n589\t\\\\This dynamical evolution of the fluid excites the modes of the quantum field, which is supposed\n590\tto be in its vacuum state before the process of formation of the sonic hole begins, \n591\tyielding nontrivial expectation\n592\tvalues for the quantum PEMT. At late times these may be approximated by\n593\t$\\langle T^{(2)}_{ab}\\rangle $ in the Unruh state evaluated \n594\tin this background. \\\\\n595\t% The trace part is exactly known and given by calulating eq. (\\ref{traccia}). \n596\t% The other two indipendent components, being not exactly known, will be approximated \n597\t% by the Polyakov stress tensor. This slightly overextimates the evaporation flux by \n598\t% neglecting the backscattering of the phonons caused by the potential barrier induced \n599\t% by the presence of the dilaton \\cite{bafa5}. \n600\t% This kind of approximation is quite common in the gravitational black hole case.\n601\t\n602\tWe introduce a set of null coordinates\n603\t\\bea\n604\t\\label{Unull}\n605\tx^-&=&c\\left( t-\\int \\frac{dz}{c+v}\\right)\\ ,\\\\\n606\t\\label{Vnull}\n607\tx^+&=&c\\left( t+\\int \\frac{dz}{c-v}\\right)\\ .\n608\t\\eea\n609\tIn terms of these coordinates the acoustic metric is \n610\t\\be\n611\tg_{ab}^{(2)}=-\\frac{\\r}{c}\\frac{c^2-v^2}{c^2}\\left(\n612\t\\begin{array}{cc}\n613\t0&\\half\\\\\n614\t\\half&0\n615\t\\end{array}\n616\t\\right)\n617\t\\ee \n618\twith $a,b=x_+,x_-$ and the quantum part in eq. (\\ref{back1}) reads\n619\t\\be\n620\t\\label{Tsum}\n621\t-\\frac{1}{c}(\\langle T_{tz}\\rangle +v\\langle T_{zz}\\rangle )\n622\t=-c^2\\left[-\\frac{\\langle T_{--}\\rangle }{(c+v)^2}\n623\t+\\frac{\\langle T_{++}\\rangle }{(c-v)^2}\\right]\\ .\n624\t\\ee\n625\tThe Polyakov $\\langle T_{--}\\rangle$ in the Unruh state is \\cite{bd}\n626\t\\be\n627\t\\label{TUU}\n628\t\\langle T_{--}\\rangle =-\\frac{\\hbar}{12\\pi}C^\\half C^{-\\half}_{,--}+\\frac{\\hbar\\kappa^2}{48\\pi}\\ ,\n629\t\\ee\n630\twhereas\n631\t\\be\n632\t\\label{TVV}\n633\t\\langle T_{++}\\rangle =-\\frac{\\hbar}{12\\pi}C^\\half C^{-\\half}_{,++}\\ .\n634\t\\ee\n635\tHere the conformal factor of the metric $C$ is\n636\t\\be\n637\tC=\\frac{\\r}{c}\\frac{c^2-v^2}{c^2}\n638\t\\ee\n639\tand $\\k$ is related to the surface gravity $k$ on the horizon\n640\t\\be\n641\tk=c^2\\k=\\left. c\\frac{d}{dz}v\\right|_H\\ .\n642\t\\ee\n643\tFor our particular chioce of $A(z)$ (see eq.(\\ref{area})), the surface gravity is \n644\t$k=c^2\\k=c^2\\sqrt{\\beta/A_0}$. The trace $\\langle T^{(2)}\\rangle$ is completely anomalous\n645\tand is given by \n646\t\\be \\label{traza}\n647\t\\langle T^{(2)}\\rangle \\frac{\\hbar}{24\\pi}R^{(2)} \\ee\n648\twhere $R^{(2)}$ is the Ricci scalar for the metric $g_{ab}^{(2)}$. \n649\t\\\\Note also that in the Unruh state $\\langle T_{--}\\rangle$ \n650\tis regular on the horizon (where $v=-c$) \n651\tmaking the r.h.s. of eq. (\\ref{Tsum}) finite.\n652\t\\\\Explicit calculation of the components of $\\langle T_{ab}^{(2)}\\rangle$ \n653\tare given in Appendix I. We recall here only the asymptotic limits\n654\t\\bea \\label{flujo}\n655\t\\left. \\langle T_{--}\\rangle \\right|_{z\\rightarrow \\infty}&=&\\frac{\\hbar\\kappa^2}{48\\pi}\\ ,\\\\\n656\t\\left. \\langle T_{++}\\rangle \\right|_{z\\rightarrow 0}&=&-\\frac{\\hbar\\kappa^2}{48\\pi}\\ .\\nonumber\n657\t\\eea\n658\t\n659\t%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%\n660\t\n661\t\\sect{The backreaction equations near the horizon}\n662\t\n663\t\n664\tAs said before our aim is to find the first order correction in $\\hbar$ to the \n665\tclassical sonic black hole solution $\\r(z),v(z)$ described in eqs. \n666\t(\\ref{rho})-(\\ref{z2}). To this end we define the quantum corrected velocity potential and density by\n667\t\\bea\n668\t\\f_B&=&\\f(z)+\\epsilon \\f_1(z,t)\\ ,\\\\\n669\t\\r_B&=&\\r(z)+\\epsilon \\r_1(z,t)\\ ,\n670\t\\eea\n671\twhere the subscript ``B\" stays for backreaction, $v=\\p_z \\f$ and we have introduced a dimensionless \n672\texpansion parameter $\\epsilon=\\hbar/(|D|A_0)$.  \n673\tThese values are found by solving the backreaction eqs. (\\ref{eqbackA}), \n674\t(\\ref{eqbackB}) linearized in $\\epsilon$\n675\t\\bea\n676\t\\label{EQ1}\n677\t&&\\epsilon\\left[A\\dot{\\r}_1+\\p_z\\left(A(\\r_1 v+\\r\\p_z \\f_1)\\right)\\right]=\n678\tc^2 \\p_z\\left[ -\\frac{\\langle T_{--}\\rangle }{(c+v)^2}+\n679\t\\frac{\\langle T_{++}\\rangle }{(c-v)^2}\\right]\\equiv \\epsilon F_2(z)\\ , \\\\\n680\t \\label{EQ2}\n681\t&& \\epsilon \\left[A(\\dot{\\f}_1+v\\p_z\\f_1+\\frac{c^2}{\\r}\\r_1)\\right] \n682\t=\\frac{\\langle T^{(2)}\\rangle }{2}\n683\t\\equiv \\epsilon G_2(z)\\ . \n684\t\\eea\n685\tThe explicit expressions for $F_2$ and $G_2$ are given in Appendix I.\\\\\n686\tFrom eq. (\\ref{EQ2}) one can obtain $\\r_1$\n687\t\\be\n688\t\\label{rho1}\n689\t\\r_1=\\frac{\\r}{c^2}\\left[ \\frac{G_2}{A}-\\dot{\\f}_1-v \\f_1' \\right]\\ , \n690\t\\ee\n691\twhere we indicate $'\\equiv \\p_z$.\\\\\n692\tTaking the time derivative of this equation and substituting it in the continuity \n693\teq. (\\ref{EQ1}) one obtains the following wave equation for $\\f_1$\n694\t\\bea\n695\t\\label{EQvisser}\n696\t&-\\frac{1}{v} \\ddot{\\f}_1-2\\dot{\\f}_1'-v'(1+\\frac{c^2}{v^2})\\f_1'+(\\frac{c^2}{v}-v)\\f_1''=&\\nonumber\\\\\n697\t&=\\left[\\frac{c^2 F_2}{D}-\\left(\\frac{G_2}{A}\\right)'\\right]\\equiv H(z)\\ .& \n698\t\\eea\n699\tThe l.h.s. is simply proportional to $\\nabla_a^{(2)}(\\frac{A\\rho}{c}\\nabla^{(2)a}\\f_1)$ \n700\tand the r.h.s. $H(z)$ represents the \n701\tquantum source evaluated for the classical static solution. \\\\ \\noindent\n702\tWe are mainly interested on the fate of the sonic horizon, so we will solve the wave \n703\tequation (\\ref{EQvisser}) near $z=0$. To this end we need an expansion of the \n704\tbackground quantities $\\r$ and $v$, and hence \n705\t$\\langle T^{(2)}_{ab}\\rangle $, for $\\kappa z\\ll 1$. \n706\tThe results of this tedious calculation are given in Appendix II. \n707\tWe give here only the final results. Eq. (\\ref{EQvisser}) becomes\n708\t\\bea\n709\t\\label{EQvisser1}\n710\t&-\\frac{1}{c}(1+\\kappa z) \\ddot{\\f}_1-2\\dot{\\f}_1'-2c\\kappa (1+\\frac{2}{3}\\kappa z)\\f_1'-2c\\kappa z\\f_1''=&\\nonumber\\\\\n711\t&=H_0+ H_1 \\kappa z\\ ,& \n712\t\\eea\n713\twhere\n714\t\\bea\n715\t\\label{H}\n716\tH_0&\\simeq& 0.038 \\frac{\\kappa^3 c^2 A_0}{\\pi}\\ , \\\\\n717\tH_1&\\simeq& 1.128  \\frac{\\kappa^3 c^2 A_0}{\\pi }\\ .\n718\t\\eea\n719\tWe shall write the solution in the following form\n720\t\\be\n721\t\\label{psi1}\n722\t\\f_1=f_0(t)+\\k z f_1(t) +\\frac{\\k^2 z^2}{2}f_2(t)+...\n723\t\\ee\n724\twhere $f_i(t),i=1,2,3...$ are functions of $t$ only, to be determined.\\\\\n725\tThe zero order (in $\\k z$) equation is\n726\t\\be\n727\t\\label{zeroorder}\n728\t\\frac{1}{c}\\ddot{f}_0(t)-2\\k \\dot{f}_1(t)-2c\\k^2 f_1(t)=H_0\\ , \n729\t\\ee\n730\twhereas the first order equation is \n731\t\\be\n732\t\\label{firstorder}\n733\t\\frac{1}{c}\\left[ \\ddot{f}_0(t)+\\ddot{f}_1(t)-2\\k\\dot{f}_2(t)\\right]-4c\\k^2\\left[ f_2(t)+\\frac{1}{3}f_1(t)\\right]\n734\t=H_1\\ .\n735\t\\ee\n736\tWe shall now define the boundary conditions on the solution. We require that at some given \n737\ttime, let's say $t=0$, the evaporation is switched on, i.e. we require \n738\t$\\f_1(t=0)=v_1(t=0)=\\r_1(t=0)=0$. \n739\t\\\\The vanishing of $\\f_1$ and $v_1=\\p_z\\f_1 $ at $t=0$ implies from eq. (\\ref{psi1}) \n740\tthat $f_i(t=0)=0$. Remembering now the relation between $\\r_1$ and $\\f_1$ \n741\t(see eq. (\\ref{rho1})) we have\n742\t\\bea\n743\t\\r_1(t=0)=0 &\\Rightarrow& \\dot{\\f}_1(t=0)=\\frac{G_2}{A} \\qquad\\qquad \\mbox{i.e.}\\nonumber\\\\\n744\t\\k^i\\frac{\\dot{f}_i(t=0)}{i!}&=&\\left(\\frac{G_2}{A}\\right)_i \\qquad\\qquad i=0,1,2.....\n745\t\\eea\n746\twhere the expression on the r.h.s. means the coefficients of the $i$-th term of the \n747\texpansion in $z$ of $G_2/A$.\\\\\n748\tEvaluating eqs. (\\ref{zeroorder}), (\\ref{firstorder}) and the time derivative of eq. \n749\t(\\ref{zeroorder}) at $t=0$ one can obtain the following approximate expression for $\\f_1$ \n750\t(see Appendix II for details) \n751\t\\be\n752\t\\f_1=a_1 t+\\frac{a_2}{2} t^2+\\frac{a_3}{3!} t^3+....+\\k z (b_1 t+\\frac{b_2}{2} t^2+....)+\\frac{\\k^2 z^2}{2}(c_1t+...)\\ .\n753\t\\ee\n754\tThe numerical coefficients are reported in the same Appendix.\n755\t\n756\tSince we have calculated the quantum source only for the static classical metric there is no time evolution of the source\n757\titself. This limits the validity of our solution for small values of $t$ only ($c\\k t\\ll 1$). For this reason we have just given a power expansion of the functions $f_i(t)$. Therefore we are only able to predict how the backreaction starts, i.e. to connect the static fluid configuration at time $t_0=0$ to a quasi static fluid configuration at time $t_0+\\Delta t$. With this in mind we can now give the quantum correction to the velocity field\n758\t\\be\n759\tv_1(z,t)=\\k b_1 t+(\\k z)c_1\\k t=\\k t (b_1+c_1\\k z)\\ .\n760\t\\ee\n761\tNote that $b_1>0$ (see  Appendix II) and being $\\k z  \\ll 1$ for the validity of our \n762\tsolution, we can conclude that $v_1>0$. The background velocity is negative, so we conclude \n763\tthat the backreaction has  the net effect to decrease the modulus of the velocity, \n764\ti.e. the fluid is slowing down.\\\\\n765\tThe quantum corrected velocity is therefore\n766\t\\be\n767\tv_B=v+\\epsilon v_1=-c+c\\k z -\\frac{1}{6}c\\k^2 z^2+\\epsilon(b_1+c_1\\k z)\\k t \\ .\n768\t\\ee\n769\t\\\\The acoustic horizon is defined $|v_B|=c$; this yields \n770\t\\be\n771\tz_H=-\\frac{\\epsilon \\k b_1 t}{c\\k+\\hbar c_1\\k^2t}\\simeq -\\frac{\\epsilon  b_1 t}{c}\\ .\n772\t\\ee\n773\tThis equation shows that the horizon is moving to the left with respect the classical location $z_H=0$. Therefore, as the evaporation proceeds, the hypersonic region gets smaller and smaller. \n774\tThis is the behaviour one would have naively expected.\n775\tThe coefficient $b_1$ determining the quantum \n776\tcorrection to the velocity and hence the evolution of the horizon is just the gradient\n777\tof the additional chemical potential related to the expectation value of the trace evaluated at $z=0$. This should be\n778\tcompared to the black hole case where the evolution of the horizon is determined by the energy flux\n779\t($\\dot M \\propto \\langle T^r_{\\ t}\\rangle$ in spherical symmetry).  \n780\tWhile in the latter case Hawking radiation occurs at the expense of the gravitational energy of \n781\tthe black\n782\thole, in the fluid phonons emission takes away kinetic energy from the system.\n783\t\\\\Finally, from eq. (\\ref{rho1}) we can calculate $\\r_1$\n784\t\\be\n785\t\\r_1=\\frac{\\r_0 e^{-\\half}}{c^2}(\\alpha+\\delta\\k z)t\\ , \n786\t\\ee\n787\twhere\n788\t\\bea\n789\t\\alpha&=&-a_2+c\\k b_1\\ , \\\\\n790\t\\delta&=&-b_2-a_2+c\\k c_1 \\ .\n791\t\\eea\n792\t%For $\\k z\\ll 1$, \n793\tThis yields $\\r_1<0$, i.e. $\\r_B=\\r+\\epsilon\\r_1$ is decreasing.\n794\t\n795\t%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%\n796\t\n797\t\\sect{The backreaction equation in the region $z>z_0$}\n798\t\n799\tIn the region $z>z_0$, assuming $\\k z_0\\ll 1$, the background solutions can be approximated as\n800\t\\bea\n801\tv&=&-c+c\\k z_0\\ ,\\\\\n802\t\\r&=&\\r_0 e^{-\\half}(1+\\k z_0)\\ .\n803\t\\eea\n804\tThe backreaction equation (\\ref{EQvisser}) becomes the simple flat space wave equation\n805\t\\be\n806\t\\label{EQflat}\n807\t\\p_-\\p_+\\f_1=0\n808\t\\ee\n809\tSince in this region $\\langle T^{(2)}\\rangle =\\langle T_{+-}\\rangle =0$ \n810\tand $\\langle T_{--}\\rangle =const$, then $F_2=G_2=0$.\\\\\n811\tThe null coordinates $x^-,x^+$ are defined as follows (see eqs. (\\ref{Unull}), (\\ref{Vnull})) \n812\t\\bea\n813\t\\label{Uflat}\n814\tx^-&=&c\\left(t-\\frac{z}{c\\k z_0}\\right)\\ ,\\\\\n815\tx^+&=&c\\left(t+\\frac{z}{2c-c\\k z_0}\\right)\\ .\n816\t\\eea\n817\tThe most general solution of (\\ref{EQflat}) is a linear combination of two arbitrary \n818\tfunctions of the kind $\\xi(x^-)$ and $\\eta(x^+)$. \n819\t\n820\tThe source term given by the quantum pseudo stress tensor is discontinuous in $z=z_0$, \n821\tso our model resembles a sandwich of space-time regions glued across  singular hypersurfaces.\n822\tWe can find a solution of (\\ref{EQflat}) for $z>z_0$ by requiring continuity for the \n823\t$v_1(z,t)$ field across the boundary $z=z_0$. \n824\tBecause of the discontinuity in $\\langle T_{ab}^{(2)}\\rangle $,\n825\tthere is no way to make $v_1$ and $\\r_1$ simultaneously continuous across $z_0$. \n826\tOur choice leads to a quantum corrected acoustic metric wich is continuous in $z=z_0$ up to a conformal factor.\\\\\n827\tFor $z<z_0$ we have\n828\t\\be\n829\tv_1(z,t)=(b_1+c_1 \\k z)\\k t\n830\t\\ee\n831\tand therefore\n832\t\\be\n833\tv_1(z_0,t)=(b_1+c_1 \\k  z_0)\\k t \\ . \n834\t\\ee\n835\tAs seen from the curved space point of view, \n836\tthe $z=z_0$ surface is a timelike surface of the acoustic metric of eq. (\\ref{metric2}). \n837\tIt is crossed in the future only by outgoing rays.\\\\\n838\tTherefore for $z>z_0$ the solution of the wave equation assumes a retarded ``Vaidya form\" \n839\t$\\f_1=\\f_1(x^-)$. Now from eq. (\\ref{Uflat})\n840\t\\be\n841\tv_1=\\p_z\\f_1(x^-)=-\\frac{1}{\\k z_0}\\p_-\\f_1\\equiv F(x^-)\\ . \n842\t\\ee\n843\tTaking into account that $x^-(t=0,z=z_0)=-1/k\\equiv x^-_0$, $F(x^-)$ can be approximated as\n844\t\\be\n845\tF(x^-)=l(x^--x^-_0)\\Theta(x^--x^-_0)+O((x^--x^-_0)^2) \\ , \n846\t\\ee\n847\twhere $l$ is a constant to be fixed by requiring continuity in $z=z_0$:\n848\t\\be\n849\t\\left. F(x^-)\\right|_{z=z_0}=lct=v_1(z_0,t)=(b_1+c\\k z_0)\\k t \\ , \n850\t\\ee\n851\tso that\n852\t\\be\n853\tl=\\frac{\\k}{c}(b_1+c_1\\k z_0)\\ , \n854\t\\ee\n855\twhich is positive definite.\\\\\n856\tTherefore for $z>z_0$, $x^->x^-_0$, we have\n857\t\\be\n858\tv_1=v_1(x^-)=\\frac{1}{c}(\\k b_1+c_1\\k^2 z_0)(x^--x^-_0)+...\\ , \n859\t\\ee\n860\twhereas for $x^-<x^-_0$ it vanishes identically.\\\\The quantum corrected velocity field reads therefore, for $z>z_0$,\n861\t\\be\n862\tv_B=v+\\hbar v_1=-c(1-\\k z_0)+\\frac{\\k}{c}(b_1+c_1\\k z_0)(x^--x^-_0)\\ ,\n863\t\\ee\n864\tshowing a velocity decreasing in modulus  with the advanced time $x^-$.\\\\\n865\tIntegrating $v_1=\\p_z\\f_1(x^-)$ one can get $\\f_1(x^-)$\n866\t\\be\n867\t\\f_1=-\\frac{\\k z_0}{2c}(\\k b_1+c_1\\k^2 z_0)(x^--x^-_0)^2\n868\t\\ee\n869\tand from it\n870\t\\be\n871\t\\r_1=\\frac{\\r}{c^2}(-\\dot{\\f}_1-vv_1)\n872\t=\\frac{\\r_0 e^{-\\half}}{c^2}(1+\\k z_0)(\\k b_1+c_1\\k^2 z_0)(x^--x^-_0)\\Theta(x^--x^-_0)\\ , \n873\t\\ee\n874\twhich increases in terms of the advanced time.\n875\t\\\\As already said $\\r_1$ cannot be made continuous across $z=z_0$. \n876\tEvaluating the limits from both sides of the hypersurface $z=z_0$ one can find the jump in $\\r_1$\n877\t\\be\n878\t\\Delta \\r_1=\\frac{\\r_0 e^{-\\half}}{c^2}[a_2+\\k z_0(\\k b_1+b_2+a_2)ct]\n879\t \\ . \\ee\n880\t\n881\t%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%\n882\t\n883\t\\sect{The backreaction equation in $z<-z_0$}\n884\t"}]},"uuid":"59c03983-5d91-44ac-916f-54060af3eadd","timestamp":"2026-08-15T19:39:31.016Z","sourceToolAssistantUUID":"5b640244-2b88-4692-8377-a532f6b23140","userType":"external","entrypoint":"claude-desktop","cwd":"/Users/johnroehm/Programming/PythonEnvironments/Physics/Fluid-Based-Physics-Research/SK_EFT_Hawking","sessionId":"6cf37aa2-f1c7-4e33-a712-f17c2d75d99b","version":"2.1.229","gitBranch":"HEAD","slug":"swift-singing-llama"}

Now the null coordinates are\n886\t\\bea\n887\tx^-&=&c\\left(t+\\frac{z}{c\\k z_0}\\right)\\ ,\\\\\n888\tx^+&=&c\\left(t+\\frac{z}{2c+c\\k z_0}\\right)\\ .\n889\t\\eea\n890\tAs one can see from the acoustic metric (\\ref{metric2}), the surface $z=-z_0$ is now a spacelike surface; it is crossed in\n891\tthe future direction from both ingoing $x^+=const$ and outgoing $x^-=const$ characteristics of the wave equation. So the\n892\tsolution will depend on both $x^-$ and $x^+$. \n893\t\n894\tThe classical background quantities are now for $z<-z_0$\n895\t\\bea\n896\t\\label{vz0}\n897\tv&=&-c-c\\k z_0\\ , \\\\\n898\t\\label{rhoz0}\n899\t\\r&=&\\r_0 e^{-\\half}(1-\\k z_0)\\ . \n900\t\\eea\n901\tThe boundary conditions we will impose to find the solution in this region are the \n902\tcontinuity for both $v_1$ and $\\r_1$. Unlike the $z=z_0$ case, here this is possible being $z=-z_0$ a spacelike surface.   Now we impose continuity of $v_1$\n903\t\\be\n904\t\\label{psi1z0}\n905\t\\p_z\\f_1(-z_0^-)=\\p_z\\f_1(-z_0^+)\\equiv \\varphi_1(ct)\\ ,\n906\t\\ee\n907\twhere the r.h.s. is calculated on the solution obtained in Section 5. \n908\tContinuity of $\\r_1$ reads\n909\t\\be\n910\t\\left. \\frac{\\r}{c^2}[-\\dot{\\f}_1-v\\p_z\\f_1]\\right|_{z=-z_0^-}=\n911\t\\frac{\\r}{c^2}\\left[\\frac{G_2}{A}-\\dot{\\f}_1-v\\p_z\\f_1\\right]\\ . \n912\t\\ee\n913\tBeing the background quantities (\\ref{vz0}), (\\ref{rhoz0}) continuous across $z=-z_0$ \n914\tand taking account of eq. (\\ref{psi1z0}) we require\n915\t\\be\n916\t\\p_z\\f_1(-z_0^-)\n917\t=\\left. \\left(\\dot{\\f}_1-\\frac{G_2}{A}\\right)\\right|_{z=-z_0^+}\\equiv c\\varphi_2(ct)\\ .\n918\t\\ee\n919\tFrom Section 5\n920\t\\bea\n921\t\\varphi_1(ct)&=&\\frac{\\k}{c}(b_1-c_1\\k z_0)t\\ , \\\\\n922\tc\\varphi_2(ct)&=&\\left( \\frac{a_2}{c}-\\frac {b_2\\k z_0}{c}\\right) ct\n923\t\\eea\n924\tand using standard technique for solving the wave equation one eventually arrives at\n925\t\\bea\n926\tv_1&=&\\left[ \\frac{\\k^2z_0}{2c}(b_1-c_1\\k z_0)-\\frac{1}{2c^2}(a_2-b_2\\k\n927\tz_0)\\right]\\left[(x^--x^-_0)\\Theta(x^--x^-_0)\\right. \\nonumber \\\\\n928\t&&\\left. -(x^+-x^+_0)\\Theta(x^+ -x^+_0)\\right]\n929\t+\\frac{\\k}{c}(b_1-c_1\\k z_0)(x^- -x^-_0)\\Theta(x^--x^-_0)\\ , \n930\t\\eea\n931\twhere we have defined\n932\t\\bea\n933\tx^-_0&=&x^-(z=-z_0,t=0)=\\frac{1}{\\k}\\\\\n934\tx^+_0&=&x^+(z=-z_0,t=0)=-\\frac{z_0}{2+\\k z_0}\\ . \n935\t\\eea\n936\tSo we have a Vaidya ingoing solution for $x^-<x^-_0$\n937\t\\be\n938\tv_1=-\\left[ \\frac{\\k z_0}{2c}(\\k b_1-z_0\\k^2 c_1)-\\frac{1}{2c^2}(a_2-\\k z_0\n939\tb_2)\\right](x^+-x^+_0)\\Theta(x^+-x^+_0)\\ , \n940\t\\ee\n941\twhence for $x^->x^-_0$\n942\t\\bea\n943\tv_1&=&\\left[ \\frac{\\k z_0}{c}(\\k b_1-c_1\\k^2 z_0)-\\frac{1}{c^2}(a_2-b_2\\k z_0) \\frac{z+z_0}{\\k z_0(2+\\k z_0)}\n944\t+ \\right.\\nonumber\\\\\n945\t&&\\left. +\\frac{\\k}{c}(b_1-c_1\\k z_0)(x^--x^-_0)\\right]\\ . \n946\t\\eea\n947\tIn a similar way we obtain\n948\t\\bea\n949\t&&\\r_1 =\\frac{\\r}{c^2}\\left\\{ (b_1-c_1\\k z_0)(x^--x^-_0)\\Theta(x^--x^-_0) \n950\t +\\left[ \\frac{\\k^2z_0}{2}(b_1-c_1\\k z_0)- \\right.\\right. \\nonumber\\\\ \n951\t && \\left.\\left. -\\half(a_2-b_2\\k\n952\tz_0)\\right]\n953\t\\left[(x^--x^-_0)\\Theta(x^- -x^-_0)-(x^+ -x^+_0)\\Theta(x^+ -x^+_0)\\right]\\right\\}\n954\t.\\;\\;\\;\\;\\;\\;\\;\\;\\;\\;\n955\t\\eea\n956\t\n957\t\n958\t%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%\n959\t\n960\t\\sect{The fate of the acoustic black hole}\n961\t\n962\tThe aim of this paper was to face the backreaction problem for acoustic black holes.\\\\\n963\tFirst we have found the equations for the fluid driven by the linear quantum fluctuations, \n964\ti.e. the linearized ``backreaction equations\". \n965\t\\\\In a lower dimensional case, keeping the Polyakov approximation for the \n966\tstress tensor, we have solved\n967\tthese equations near the horizon, under the assumption that the quantum source \n968\tcorresponds to the pseudo stress tensor of the quantum fields evaluated for the static classical background. \n969\t\\\\The information we can gain is just preliminary: we obtain an indication on how the quantum solution starts to depart from the classical configuration, once the quantum effects are switched on. \n970\t\\\\It's not possible to do anything better even for the gravitational black hole \n971\tevaporation. However very interesting\n972\tindications seem to emerge even from this simplified model.  \\\\\n973\tWe have shown that the sonic horizon moves to the left with respect to the nozzle and the hypersonic region shrinks.\n974\tFrom the expression of the quantum corrected fluid velocity\n975\t\\be\n976\tv_B=-c+c\\k z -\\frac{1}{6}c\\k^2 z^2 +\\epsilon(b_1+c_1\\k z)\\k t\n977\t\\ee\n978\tand the equation for the horizon\n979\t\\be\n980\t\\label{zH}\n981\tz_H=-\\epsilon\\frac{b_1}{c} t\n982\t\\ee\n983\tone can evaluate how the emission temperature of these quasi static configuration varies \n984\twith time, i.e.\n985\t\\bea\n986\t T&=&\\left. \\frac{\\hbar c}{2\\pi }\\frac{\\p v_B}{\\p z}\\right|_{z_H}=\\nonumber\\\\\n987\t&&=\\frac{\\hbar c}{2\\pi  }\\left( \\k-\\frac{1}{3}\\k^2z_H+\\frac{\\epsilon \\k^2 c_1}{c}t\\right)\\ . \n988\t\\eea\n989\tThis, using eq.(\\ref{zH}), yields\n990\t\\bea\n991\t\\label{Tsonic}\n992\tT&=&\\frac{\\hbar c}{2\\pi }\\k \\left[ 1+\\frac{\\epsilon \\k}{c}\\left(\\frac{b_1}{3}+c_1\\right)t\\right]=\\nonumber\\\\\n993\t&&=\\frac{\\hbar c}{2\\pi }\\k \\left[ 1-\\frac{563}{720\\pi}\\epsilon \\k^3 c A_0t\\right]\\ .\n994\t\\eea\n995\tThis expression is rather significative: it tells us that the emission temperature of the sonic black hole decreases in time. Unlike Schwarzschild black holes, the sonic black hole gets cooler as it evaporates. Its behaviour is therefore  much more similar to a Reissner-Nordstr\\\"om black hole.\n996\t\n997\tIt's very interesting to try to extrapolate this behaviour in time. From eq. (\\ref{Tsonic}) \n998\twe have\n999\t\\be\n1000\t\\Delta T\\propto-\\k^4 c^2 A_0 \\Delta t\\simeq \\propto -T^4\\Delta t \\ . \n1001\t\\ee\n1002\tThis yields approximatively\n1003\t\\be\n1004\tt\\sim \\frac{1}{T^3}\\ . \n1005\t\\ee\n1006\tThis implies that as the sonic black hole radiates, its temperature decreases reaching \n1007\tasymptotically zero value in an infinite time. \n1008\t\n1009\tFor a near extremal Reissner-Nordstr\\\"om black hole ($r_+\\simeq M\\simeq |Q|$) a similar analysis yields\n1010\t\\bea\n1011\t\\frac{d M}{d t}&\\simeq & -A_HT_H^4\\propto -Q^2(M-Q)^2 Q^2\\ , \\\\ \n1012\t\\frac{1}{M-Q}&=&t\\sim \\frac{1}{T^2}\\ . \n1013\t\\eea\n1014\tSo sonic balck holes resemble  near extremal R-N black holes. \n1015\tThe end-state of the evaporation process corresponds in both cases to a zero temperature  configuration, \n1016\treached asymptotically in time.\n1017\t\\\\One should mention that other analog models like a thin film \n1018\tof ${}^3 He\\mbox{-A}$ with a moving domain wall \\cite{jacobson} seem to show \n1019\ta non-vanishing end-temperature of the evaporation process.\n1020\t\\\\In a similar way one can treat sonic black holes formed by a Bose-Einstein condensate \\cite{garayvisser}. \n1021\tThe major difference comes from the fact that the \n1022\tsound velocity $c$ is not constant, but proportional to $\\r^\\half$. This will be discussed\n1023\telsewhere. \n1024\t\n1025\t%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%\n1026\t\n1027\t\\sect{Conclusion}\n1028\t\n1029\tThe basic question which the analysis presented here leaves unanswered is to what extent\n1030\tdoes the behaviour we have obtained for the quantum corrected evolution depend on the\n1031\tlinear dispersion relation used (free scalar field to describe phonons), which ignores short\n1032\tdistance corrections due to the molecular structure of the fluid.\n1033\tThe same uncertainty exists for any study in curved space quantum field theory which involves \n1034\thigh frequency modes like the Hawking effect or in general renormalization calculations. \n1035\tOne does not know how the yet unknown behaviour of the spacetime at the Planck scale may\n1036\tinfluence the results. So far many studies have been devoted to investigate the robustness of\n1037\tthe thermal radiation predicted by Hawking both in the gravitational context and in the\n1038\tanalogue models. Looking at 2D models one has mainly analyzed the behaviour of the Bogolubov\n1039\t$\\beta_w$ coefficient giving the created particles number once nonlinear\n1040\tdispersion relations are introduced in the high frequency regime. This is supposed \n1041\tto model the breaking of local Lorentz (or Galilean, in the analogue model context) invariance here\n1042\texpected. The scale at which this happens is the Planck scale for gravity, whereas\n1043\tfor sonic black holes it is the intermolecular size. \n1044\tAs a result of these studies there is now some consensus (see however the recent paper\n1045\t\\cite{unsc} where interesting counterexamples are given) that the $\\beta_w$ coefficient is\n1046\tbasically unaffected by the dispersion relation \\cite{jacobson2}. However no one knows yet \n1047\twhat happens to observables like $\\langle T_{\\mu\\nu}\\rangle$, which are in addition sensible\n1048\tto the regularization scheme used. \n1049\tIn a pure 2D context and for massless scalar fields, Jacobson \\cite{jacobson3} has argued that,\n1050\twithin a covariant regularization, no significant deviation from the usual expression for the\n1051\ttrace anomaly (eq. (\\ref{traza})) and the flux (eq. \\ref{flujo})) are expected \n1052\tif one introduces a cutoff at high frequencies.\n1053\tHowever, for the hydrodynamical system we have considered, covariance is a symmetry of the \n1054\tphonons low energy effective theory only, which is broken \n1055\tat short distance.  \n1056\tHence non covariant terms depending on the microscopic physics are expected to show up in the effective action\n1057\tand are crucial for a correct description of the unperturbed quantum vacuum of the fluid. \n1058\tHowever the expectation values $\\langle T_{\\mu\\nu}\\rangle$ entering the backreaction equations \n1059\t(\\ref{eqbackA}, \\ref{eqbackB}) \n1060\tdo not represent the energy momentum of the fluid quantum vacuum.\n1061\tThey describe instead the perturbation of the stationary vacuum (whose energy is strictly \n1062\tzero \\cite{volovik}) induced by inhomogeneities and by the time dependent formation\n1063\tof the sonic hole which triggers the phonons emission. In this paper we have assumed that these deviations can be computed \n1064\twithin the low energy theory. This situation is not unusual. \n1065\t%In the traditional Casimir effect it is well known that the final finite result for the vacuum energy does not depend\n1066\t%on the high energy frequency modes and is calculated directly from the low energy theory only.\n1067\t%There are some examples for quantum liquids where this holds (see G. Volovik in Ref. \\cite{libro}).    \n1068\tCasimir effects are well known examples of vacuum disturbances caused by the presence of boundaries.\n1069\tIt happens that the Casimir energy is often (but not always, \n1070\tsee G. Volovik in Ref. \\cite{libro})\n1071\tindependent on the microscopic physics and can be calculated within the framework of the low\n1072\tenergy theory. This happens because, while low frequency modes are reflected by the \n1073\tboundaries, for the high energy\n1074\tones the wall is transparent.  They produce a divergent contribution to the vacuum energy which \n1075\tis canceled by a proper regularization scheme and does not affect the finite result. We have assumed\n1076\tthat a similar decoupling happens for the acoustic black hole.   \n1077\tThe check of our hypothesis would require an analysis of the quantum system within \n1078\tthe microscopic theory which takes into account\n1079\tthe time dependent non homogeneous formation of the sonic hole. \n1080\tThis is for the moment beyond computational capability.\n1081\t%Unfortunately no similar restriction seems to hold in 4D.     \n1082\t\\\\More efforts are therefore necessary to fully understand the role played by the high-frequency\n1083\tmodes in the above scenarios; in particular what is needed is a proper description of the way these\n1084\tmodes interact with the underlying medium.\n1085\t\\\\To this end the study of black hole analogue models seems much more promising, since there the\n1086\tunderlying physics is at least in principle known. Progress in this area may then be used as\n1087\t``theoretical laboratory'' for ideas to be exported and tested in quantum gravity. \n1088\t\\\\Given the the present limited understanding, our work is of course not the end story but it should\n1089\tbe regarded simply as a first attempt to attack the backreaction problem in sonic black holes, an\n1090\tattempt performed using available technical tools developed in quantum field theory in curved\n1091\tspace. \n1092\t\\\\It is obvious that more detailed analysis are needed and will hopefully be performed in the not\n1093\ttoo distant future. However being the behaviour we have found for the evolution of a sonic hole\n1094\tphysically quite reasonable, we would expect these features to be confirmed. \n1095\t\n1096\t\\vspace{1cm}\n1097\t{\\bf Acknowledgements}\n1098\t\n1099\tWe thank R. Emparan, L. Garay, T. Jacobson, M. Maio, R. Parentani and J. Russo \n1100\tfor useful comments and E. Berti for help with the figure. \n1101\t\n1102\t\\appendix\n1103\t\\section{Appendix I}\n1104\tIn this appendix we give the relevant expressions needed to evaluate the r.h.s. of the backreaction equations.\\\\\n1105\t \n1106\tThe stress tensor components are\n1107\t\\bea\n1108\tT^{(2)}_{--}&=&-\\frac{\\hbar}{12\\pi}\\frac{(c^2-v^2)}{4c^4}\n1109\t\\left[\\left(-\\frac{\\r''}{2\\r}+\\frac{3}{4}\\frac{{\\r'}^2}{\\r^2}\\right)(c^2-v^2)\\right.\n1110\t+\\nonumber\\\\\n1111\t&&\\left. \n1112\t+{v'}^2+vv''+\\frac{(vv')^2}{c^2-v^2}\\right]+\\frac{\\hbar \\k^2}{48\\pi}\\ , \n1113\t\\\\ T^{(2)}_{++}&=&T^{(2)}_{--}-\\frac{\\hbar \\k^2}{48\\pi} \\ . \n1114\t\\eea\n1115\tThe anomalous trace is given by\n1116\t\\be\n1117\tT^{(2)}=\\frac{\\hbar}{24\\pi}R^{(2)}\\ , \n1118\t\\ee\n1119\twhere\n1120\t\\be\n1121\tR=-\\frac{1}{\\r c}\\left[\\left(\\frac{\\r''}{\\r}-\\frac{{\\r'}^2}{\\r^2}\\right)(c^2-v^2)\n1122\t-\\left(\\frac{2vv'\\r'}{\\r}+2{v'}^2+2vv''\\right)\\right]\\ .\\ee \n1123\t%(\\nabla\\phi)^2&=&\\frac{(c^2-v^2)}{\\r c}\\left(\\half\\frac{v'}{v}\\right)^2\\ . \n1124\t%\\Box \\phi&=&\\frac{1}{c\\r}\\p_z\\left[(c^2-v^2)\\half\\frac{v'}{v}\\right]\\ . \n1125\t%\\eea\n1126\tOne needs an expansion of the background velocity field till  the fifth order in $\\k z$\n1127\t\\be\n1128\t\\label{A1}\n1129\tv\\simeq -c+c\\k z-\\frac{1}{6}c \\k^2 z^2-\\frac{11}{36}c \\k^3 z^3\n1130\t+\\frac{77}{1080}c\\k^4 z^4+\\frac{769}{4320}c\\k^5z^5\\ . \n1131\t\\ee\n1132\tSimilarly for the energy density\n1133\t\\be\n1134\t\\label{A2}"}]},"uuid":"875630a8-ea03-4b48-a572-70894fe2dd73","timestamp":"2026-08-15T19:39:35.947Z","sourceToolAssistantUUID":"27089e1e-b109-48b5-b7e9-fedec8678b60","userType":"external","entrypoint":"claude-desktop","cwd":"/Users/johnroehm/Programming/PythonEnvironments/Physics/Fluid-Based-Physics-Research/SK_EFT_Hawking","sessionId":"6cf37aa2-f1c7-4e33-a712-f17c2d75d99b","version":"2.1.229","gitBranch":"HEAD","slug":"swift-singing-llama"}

Here is the section.\n\n```latex\n\\section{The regime partition: which black holes the substrate's thermodynamics reaches}\n\\label{sec:regime}\n\nThe substrate's black-hole thermodynamics does not describe one family of\nholes. It describes two, separated at a definite mass. There is a positive\ncritical mass $M_c$, fixed by the microscopic parameters alone, such that a\nhole sits on the Schwarzschild branch exactly when its mass exceeds $M_c$ and\non the extremality branch exactly when its mass falls below it. The two\nbranches move their temperatures in opposite directions as they radiate, and\nthey end in different places. This is a theorem about the substrate, proved\nfrom the definitions of $M_c$ and of the branch classifier, and it is the\nstatement that fixes the scope of everything the rest of this section says\nabout evaporation.\n\n\\paragraph{Scope of the formal structure.}\nThe structure carrying this result is named for the Bardeen--Carter--Hawking\nfour laws of black-hole mechanics~\\cite{BardeenCarterHawking1973}, and it\ncarries less than that name suggests. The second law is present as a\nconstraint: an externally supplied entropy-current divergence is required to\nbe non-negative, $\\partial_\\mu s^\\mu \\ge 0$, on a horizon of positive area.\nThe first law is present only as a side condition, namely the positivity of\nthe emergent Newton constant $G_N^{\\mathrm{emerg}}$ that its coupling\n$1/(8\\pi G_N^{\\mathrm{emerg}})$ requires, together with, on the extremality\nbranch, the algebraic form of the substrate-response coefficient\n$\\delta_{\\mathrm{ADW}}$. The Smarr relation itself is not encoded. The zeroth\nlaw and the third law carry no field at all. Constancy of the surface gravity\non the horizon needs Killing-vector and horizon-generator machinery, and the\nIsrael strong form of the third law needs an affine-time integral formalism;\nthe formalization possesses neither, and states both absences rather than\nfilling the slots with vacuous placeholders. What follows is therefore a\nclassification theorem plus a sign statement, not a formal derivation of\nblack-hole mechanics.\n\n\\subsection{The critical mass and the classification}\n\\label{sec:regime-theorem}\n\nThe critical mass is\n\\begin{equation}\n\\label{eq:Mc-regime}\nM_c \\;=\\; \\frac{N_f\\,\\Lambda_{\\mathrm{UV}}}{12\\pi\\,\\alpha_{\\mathrm{ADW}}}\\,,\n\\end{equation}\na ratio of the flavour content, the ultraviolet cutoff and the emergent-gravity\ncoefficient, each of which is specified independently in the microscopic sector.\nIt is positive whenever those parameters are\n(\\texttt{BHThermodynamicsFourLaws.M\\_c\\_pos}), so the partition is never empty\non either side.\n\nThe classification is a biconditional. Writing $\\mathrm{classify}(b,p)$ for the\nbranch assigned to a hole $b$ against substrate parameters $p$,\n\\begin{equation}\n\\label{eq:regime-biconditional}\n\\mathrm{classify}(b,p) = \\text{Schwarzschild}\n\\iff M > M_c\\,,\n\\end{equation}\nwhich is \\texttt{BHThermodynamicsFourLaws.classify\\_Schwarz\\-schild\\_iff}; the\ncomplementary direction, $\\mathrm{classify}(b,p) = \\text{extremality}\n\\iff M < M_c$, is\n\\texttt{BHThermo\\-dynamicsFourLaws.classify\\_ADWExtremality\\_iff}, and the\ncrossover $M = M_c$ is its own case. The classifier is a function of the mass\ncomparison and nothing else, so the branch a hole occupies is decided by a\nsingle inequality rather than by a modelling choice.\n\nEvaluated at the natural microscopic point, where the cutoff sits at the Planck\nmass, the flavour count takes the value fixed by the Dirac sector and\n$\\alpha_{\\mathrm{ADW}}$ takes its matching value, the critical mass is a\nfraction of the Planck mass,\n\\begin{equation}\n\\label{eq:Mc-planck}\n\\frac{M_c}{M_{\\mathrm{Pl}}} \\;=\\; \\input{tables/m_c_over_planck_mass.tex}\\unskip\\,.\n\\end{equation}\nEvery astrophysical mass exceeds this by many orders of magnitude, so\n\\eqref{eq:regime-biconditional} places every astrophysical hole on the\nSchwarzschild branch without ambiguity. The extremality branch is a statement\nabout the substrate's own sub-Planckian sector, not about anything in the sky.\n\n\\subsection{Temperature on each branch}\n\\label{sec:regime-temperature}\n\nOn the Schwarzschild branch the temperature is the textbook\none~\\cite{Hawking1975}, $T_H(M) = 1/(8\\pi M)$ in units with\n$\\hbar = G = c = k_B = 1$, and it is strictly decreasing in the mass\n(\\texttt{BHThermodynamicsFourLaws.T\\_H\\_schwarz\\-schild\\_strict\\_decreasing}).\nA hole losing mass therefore heats.\n\nOn the extremality branch the substrate carries an explicit cooling evolution,\n\\begin{equation}\n\\label{eq:acoustic-cooling}\nT_H(t) \\;=\\; T_{H,0}\\,e^{-t/\\tau_{\\mathrm{cool}}}\\,,\n\\end{equation}\nstrictly decreasing in $t$ for positive $T_{H,0}$ and $\\tau_{\\mathrm{cool}}$\n(\\texttt{BHThermodynamicsFourLaws.T\\_H\\_acoustic\\_evolution\\_strict\\_de\\-creasing}).\nEquation~\\eqref{eq:acoustic-cooling} is the leading-order form of a slower\napproach to zero temperature, and its role here is to fix a sign, not a rate.\n\nThe honest form of the branch-sign statement is weaker than the two\nmonotonicity results just quoted, and it is worth stating exactly.\n\\texttt{BHThermodynamicsFourLaws.regime\\_partition\\_criterion} takes a\nhypothesis bundle in which the sign of the evaporation rate on each side of\n$M_c$ is a \\emph{field}, and it transports those fields through the\nclassification biconditional to conclude that the rate is positive whenever the\nclassifier returns the Schwarzschild branch and negative whenever it returns\nthe extremality branch. It does not derive either sign. The Schwarzschild\nmonotonicity theorem is consumed by no other declaration, and the cooling\nmonotonicity theorem is consumed only by a falsifier that rules out candidate\ndecay profiles; neither enters the partition theorem. What is proved is that\nthe sign flip, if it occurs at all, occurs exactly at $M_c$ and nowhere else.\nThat is the weakest reading of the result and the true one.\n\nUnder the same hypothesis bundle the substrate-response coefficient obeys\n$\\delta_{\\mathrm{ADW}} = (\\alpha_{\\mathrm{ADW}} - 1)\\Lambda_{\\mathrm{UV}}$ and\nvanishes precisely when $\\alpha_{\\mathrm{ADW}} = 1$\n(\\texttt{BHThermodynamicsFourLaws.delta\\_ADW\\_nonzero\\_iff\\_alpha\\_ADW\\_ne\\_one}),\nwhich converts the emergent-gravity coefficient into something a measurement of\n$\\delta_{\\mathrm{ADW}}$ could contradict.\n\n\\begin{figure}[tb]\n\\centering\n\\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth]{figures/fig_T_H_evolution_regime_partition.png}\n\\caption{The regime partition, in two panels with independent axes. Left:\nthe temperature history of each branch, with each curve normalised to its own\ninitial temperature and plotted against its own clock, the cooling time\n$\\tau_{\\mathrm{cool}}$ on the extremality branch and the evaporation time on\nthe Schwarzschild branch. The panel therefore compares directions, not\nmagnitudes: no temperature, time or mass scale is shared between the two\ncurves, and nothing in it places a superfluid horizon and an astrophysical\nhole on a common axis. Right: the substrate-response coefficient\n$\\delta_{\\mathrm{ADW}} = (\\alpha_{\\mathrm{ADW}} - 1)\\Lambda_{\\mathrm{UV}}$ in\nunits of the cutoff, plotted against $\\alpha_{\\mathrm{ADW}}$ alone. It crosses\nzero at the bare induced-gravity value $\\alpha_{\\mathrm{ADW}} = 1$ and has a\ndefinite sign on either side of it.}\n\\label{fig:regime-partition}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\subsection{Independent corroboration from laboratory analogues}\n\\label{sec:regime-analogues}\n\nNothing above depends on a laboratory system. The partition is proved from the\nsubstrate's own definitions. It is nonetheless worth asking whether the\nquestion it answers is a real one, and the analogue-gravity literature answers\nthat it is: horizons realised in the same physical medium do not share an end\nstate, so the end state has to be classified rather than assumed.\n\n\\paragraph{End temperatures in superfluid and fluid horizons.}\nJacobson and Volovik studied a planar splay soliton propagating in bulk\n$^{3}$He-A~\\cite{JacobsonVolovik1998}. Their horizon condition is one-sided:\nin the section on the horizon and ergoregion they state that the horizons\nappear in the moving soliton if $v > c_\\perp$, with the horizon location fixed\nby their Eq.~(5.2), $\\cos^2\\!\\alpha(z_h) = (v^2 - c_\\perp^2)/(v_F^2 -\nc_\\perp^2)$. Their surface gravity, Eq.~(5.7), is\n\\begin{equation}\n\\label{eq:jv-kappa}\n\\kappa \\;=\\; \\frac{v_F}{d}\\left(1 - \\frac{v^2}{v_F^2}\\right)\n\\sqrt{\\frac{1 - c_\\perp^2/v^2}{1 - c_\\perp^2/v_F^2}}\\,,\n\\end{equation}\nand the Hawking temperature is $T_H = \\hbar\\kappa/2\\pi k_B$ (their Eq.~(6.1)).\nThe radicand in~\\eqref{eq:jv-kappa} carries the factor $1 - c_\\perp^2/v^2$, so\n$\\kappa$ and therefore $T_H$ go to zero as back-reaction slows the soliton\ntoward $c_\\perp$ from above. Their discussion section says exactly this, and\nsays what it means: the Hawking temperature is fairly constant until, as $v$\napproaches $c_\\perp$, $T_H$ goes to zero, which is unlike the evaporation of a\nneutral black hole that gets hotter as it shrinks and is rather like a hole\nwith a large magnetic charge that cannot be discharged, and so cools as it\nevaporates and approaches an extremal hole. The prose and the equations agree.\nThis is a cooling horizon with a vanishing end temperature.\n\nBalbinot, Fagnocchi and Fabbri computed the back-reaction for a sonic hole in a\nLaval nozzle~\\cite{Balbinot2005PRD}. The scope of that calculation is narrow\nand the authors are explicit about it: the dimensional-reduction section\nassumes the flow is one-dimensional, and the section constructing the static\nbackground assumes further that the sound velocity is constant. In their\nconcluding section, on the fate of the acoustic black hole, the quantum\ncorrection moves the horizon and lowers the emission temperature, giving a\ntemperature that decreases linearly in time at leading order, and the\nextrapolation $t \\sim 1/T^3$ then sends the temperature to zero\nasymptotically, in infinite time. They record the resemblance to a\nnear-extremal Reissner--Nordstr\\\"om hole, whose evaporation likewise ends at a\nzero-temperature configuration reached asymptotically. This is a second\nvanishing end temperature, in a fluid rather than a superfluid. It is not a\ncondensate result, and the authors say why they are not claiming one: for a\nsonic hole formed in a Bose--Einstein condensate the sound velocity is not\nconstant but proportional to $\\rho^{1/2}$, and that case is deferred to later\nwork.\n\nJacobson and Koike supply the contrast, in a thin film of $^{3}$He-A carrying a\nmoving domain wall~\\cite{JacobsonKoike2002}. There the wall moves at\n$v < c_\\perp$ relative to the condensate, the effective speed is $c(x) =\nc_\\perp \\tanh(x/d)$, and black and white hole horizons sit where $c(x_h) = \\pm\nv$. In the subsection on the Hawking effect they obtain\n\\begin{equation}\n\\label{eq:jk-TH}\nT_H(v) \\;=\\; T_H(0)\\left(1 - \\frac{v^2}{c_\\perp^2}\\right)\\,,\n\\qquad\nT_H(0) \\;=\\; \\frac{\\hbar c_\\perp}{2\\pi d}\\,,\n\\end{equation}\nin the frame of the wall, and they give the temperature in the asymptotic frame\nof the superfluid as the Doppler-shifted\n\\begin{equation}\n\\label{eq:jk-Tsf}\nT_{H,\\mathrm{sf}} \\;=\\; T_H(0)\\left(1 + \\frac{v}{c_\\perp}\\right)\\,,\n\\end{equation}\nnoting that it is never less than $T_H(0)$. The direction of drift is a frame\nquestion and not a physical one: as radiation slows the wall, the wall-frame\ntemperature~\\eqref{eq:jk-TH} rises toward $T_H(0)$ while the superfluid-frame\ntemperature~\\eqref{eq:jk-Tsf} falls toward the same value. The frame-independent\nstatement, and the one that matters here, is that both limits are the same\nnon-vanishing constant $T_H(0)$, of order a microkelvin for their parameters.\nThe authors qualify their own model carefully, stating that they have a model\nof the background geometry and that it is not yet established that the system\nradiates at all, since Pauli blocking may terminate the process before the wall\ncomes to rest; the non-vanishing endpoint is a property of the temperature\nformula, which is what the classification question turns on. Balbinot and\nco-workers themselves draw this comparison in the concluding section cited\nabove, remarking that other analogue models such as a thin film of $^{3}$He-A\nwith a moving domain wall seem to show a non-vanishing end temperature of the\nevaporation process, and their reference for the remark is the thin-film work.\n\nThe upshot is a fact about analogue horizons and not about the substrate: the\nsame superfluid supports a bulk soliton whose horizon cools to zero and a\nthin-film domain wall whose horizon ends at a finite temperature. The material\ndoes not decide the end state; a criterion on the state does. That is\ncorroboration for the shape of the partition proved in\nSec.~\\ref{sec:regime-theorem} and Sec.~\\ref{sec:regime-temperature}, and it is\nnot evidence for the value of $M_c$, which no analogue system constrains.\n\n\\paragraph{Which substrates can induce gravity: a recorded classification.}\nThe same subsection carries a second and separate piece of bookkeeping, because\nit does the same job. Whether a condensed-matter substrate can induce gravity\nin the sense of Sakharov's programme~\\cite{Sakharov1968} is recorded here as a\nvalue on each of a list of conditions: emergent Lorentz invariance of the\neffective metric, universal coupling of all matter sectors to that one metric,\nan induced Newton constant generated by matter-loop fluctuations, and agreement\nbetween the induced cosmological term and the substrate's proper vacuum energy.\nThe list is this manuscript's own bookkeeping. It is not a criterion asserted\nunder that name by any of the works cited below, and the citations support the\nindividual entries rather than the list.\n\nFor $^{3}$He-A the entries are supported by Jannes and\nVolovik~\\cite{JannesVolovik2012}. In their section on bi-metric gravity in\nsystems with Weyl points they stress that the same effective metric governs\nboth the relativistic fermions emerging near the Weyl points and the gauge\nbosons emerging there, so that the effective gravity couples universally and\ninteracts with all matter in the same way, a consequence of the\nAtiyah--Bott--Shapiro construction; they add that the effective theory obeys\nbackground independence at the kinematical level and the equivalence principle,\nboth broken above the trans-Planckian scale of the medium. Their section on the\ncosmological constant and vacuum readjustment identifies the parameter\n$\\lambda$ that generalises the cosmological constant in this bi-metric setting\nwith the difference in proper vacuum energy between the state without gravity\nand the equilibrium state in which gravity emerges, and their concluding\nsections tie $\\lambda$ to the graviton masses and show that the cosmological\nterm itself vanishes in equilibrium.\n\nFor the acoustic condensate the entries go the other way, and the source is\nFinazzi, Liberati and Sindoni~\\cite{FinazziLiberatiSindoni2012}. In their\nanalogue-cosmological-constant section the emergent Newtonian potential obeys a\nPoisson-like equation whose source contains a term present even in the absence\nof phonons, which is the analogue cosmological constant. Their own conclusion is that this quantity\ncannot be computed within an effective theory dealing only with the emergent\ndegrees of freedom. The acoustic geometry, moreover, exists only below the\nhealing length, which they identify as the Lorentz-breaking scale; above it the\neffective geometry is not defined. The sector that fixes what gravitates in\nthis model is therefore not the sector that propagates on the effective metric,\nand the universal-coupling entry fails. Jannes and Volovik draw the same\ncontrast from the other side in their introduction and closing discussion,\nobserving that the acoustic metric obeys hydrodynamic equations that are not\ndiffeomorphism invariant, so that the analogue of the cosmological constant\nthere may differ essentially from the vacuum energy.\n\nWhat the formalization does with this is narrower than the physics just\nsummarised, and the difference should be stated in the open.
